speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FEDERAL GRANTS IN LIEU OF MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement with respect to certain proposals the government has concerning grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes. I must ask the indulgence of hon. members for the length of the statement, but the questions involved are important, and I think it is as well that hon. members should have a full statement of the reasons which prompted the government to make the proposals which it intends to make. Of course full opportunity will be afforded for discussing them when I ask for appropriate financial provisions to carry them into effect.
For some considerable time the government has had under review its policy in respect of the tax-exempt status of its real property in various municipalities throughout Canada. The present situation, which reflects the exemption from municipal taxation granted to crown property under the British
North America Act, has given rise to increasing complaints as the number and variety of federal properties have multiplied during the past few years. These complaints have been embodied in representations from such bodies as the Canadian federation of mayors and the Ontario association of mayors and reeves, as well as from individual municipalities.
The government, aware of the problems faced by at least some municipalities in financing continuing growth and expanding services, has studied these complaints with sympathy and with the utmost care. Every effort has been made to gather together the relevant data and to examine these data in the light of conditions and needs in our own country and the experience of other countries.
One of the first steps in this study was to make a preliminary survey of all federal government property in Canada. This survey took a good deal of time to complete, but it was absolutely necessary to arrive at an appreciation of the nature and magnitude of the problem.
Another phase of the study was a review of the experience and practice, in this field, of other countries of the world, particularly the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, and the Scandinavian countries. This review was most illuminating. It revealed, in practically all countries, conditions and a course of development very much like our own. In practically every country, as a result of either legislation or custom, the practice is, or at least has been at some time, to exempt from local taxation the real property of the central government. However, there has been increasing recognition that this tax exemption gives rise to a problem for the municipalities, and a number of countries have found it advisable to have their central governments assume a measure of responsibility. Nevertheless, no consistent or uniform pattern has been evolved. The problem is still under consideration in most countries, and quite a few are looking with interest to any solution which may be proposed by Canada.
While this review of the practices followed elsewhere was most helpful, none of the various solutions adopted abroad was found to be wholly applicable to Canada. A solution suitable to a closely-knit unitary state, such as the United Kingdom, cannot be applied to a federal state, such as Canada,

Crown Properties
where governmental powers are divided and where the municipality is a creature of a provincial rather than the central government. The only two countries where the central government was found to pay full rates on all its properties were the United Kingdom and Eire, both unitary states where the local governments are subordinate to and integrated with the. central government and where financial and administrative relationships are more a question of financial accounting then separate fiscal responsibility. It is significant that even in these two countries the central government has felt it necessary to maintain the right to assess its own property and thereby determine the total amount of taxes payable to municipalities. Unfortunately it was found that in the United States and the other federal states which were examined, where despite differences of size and historical development the basic ingredients of the problem are the same as in our case, no satisfactory solution has as yet been worked out.
Having obtained information on the nature and scope of the problem in Canada, and after studying the methods followed in other countries in dealing with a similar situation, the government came to the conclusion that if an acceptable solution were to be found it would have to be one that was based on consistent general principles, one that recognized the absence in Canada of any administrative connection between the central government and municipal governments, and one that would in its application be equitable to all municipalities as well as to the Canadian taxpayer.
As a first principle it was decided that the constitutional exemption of federal property from municipal taxation must be maintained. Consequently the federal grants in lieu of municipal taxes, which we propose to seek parliament's authority to make, are to be made solely as a matter of grace and are to be subject to discretionary determination by an agency of the federal government. It is proposed to set up under the treasury board a unit which will be staffed with competent men, preferably men who have had some experience in the field of municipal tax assessment or valuation of properties for tax and other purposes; and it will be the job of these officials to consult with municipal authorities and to apply as fairly as possible to the assessment of government property the same principles and practices as are being applied in the assessment of similar private properties.
I think hon. members will readily agree that we are under an obligation, in adopting a program of this sort, to avoid creating a situation whereby a few municipalities, by means of discriminatory assessment practices,

could benefit at the expense of other municipalities and the taxpayer in general. I may add that our survey of the experience of other countries revealed a universal acceptance of this general principle.
In the second place, it was decided that, to be fair to all municipalities, any federal program of this sort should recognize that the presence of federal property within a municipality normally brings certain definite benefits to the municipality. These benefits include not only the increase in local incomes and business activity resulting from the presence of federal employees who work and live within the municipality, but also the greater degree of stability given to municipal revenues by the fact that a good proportion of municipal taxpayers are in the employ of the federal government. It is not difficult to demonstrate that these benefits do accrue to municipalities which have federal property within their boundaries. Such benefits are constantly reflected in the competition which, as all hon. members know, exists amongst municipalities for new federal buildings or new federal enterprises of one sort or another. I need only refer to a recent controversy highly publicized in this community, the controversy resulting from the decision to remove the government printing bureau from Ottawa to Hull.
It has indeed been argued by some that the benefits resulting to a municipality from the presence of federal real property within the municipality are more than sufficient to compensate for any added cost of municipal services which might be occasioned by the presence of this added property. I think this contention carries the benefit theory too far, if not in all cases, at least under certain circumstances to which I shall refer more fully in a moment. However, there is sufficient in the theory, I believe, to demonstrate that in any program of federal grants in lieu of municipal taxes, it would be unfair to municipalities generally to base the grants on acceptance by the central government of responsibility for a full equivalent of ordinary taxes.
The third general principle relates to the special circumstances I referred to a moment ago, the special cases where it clearly cannot be said that the benefits derived by a municipality from the presence of federal property within its limits are more than sufficient to compensate for the added costs resulting therefrom. This special type of case is where there is an abnormally large concentration of federal property within a municipality. The studies which have been made have convinced the government that where federal property is heavily concentrated, a problem is created for the municipality because our

present municipal tax systems are not designed in such a way that they obtain for the municipal corporation as such all the benefits which accrue to the municipality at large from the presence of federal property. As everyone knows, municipal revenues are based primarily on real estate taxation and therefore may not fully reflect a substantial increase in personal incomes and business activity within the municipality which may flow from a heavy concentration of federal properties. We have therefore reached the conclusion that the key to any solution to the problem before us is the degree of concentration of federal property in a municipality; and the solution which I am about to propose is based primarily on this premise.
To be able to apply this solution, it is first of all necessary to establish a clear test of what constitutes abnormal concentration of federal property. The test which we are proposing is that anything in excess of the national average of all federal property to total municipal assessments in all municipalities in Canada shall be considered abnormal concentration. The preliminary figures we have obtained as a result of the survey of federal property I referred to at the outset of my remarks indicate that this national average is somewhere between four per cent and five per cent. For the purposes of the solution we are proposing, it has been decided to use the lower figure of four per cent, at least in the initial period. This, of course, is more favourable to the municipalities than adopting the higher figure. Later, when we have completed the work of applying the ordinary principles and practices of municipal assessment to all our federal property, we may have to revise that figure to some extent.
I am therefore glad to be able to announce that the government is prepared to seek the authority of parliament to pay annually to any municipality, as a matter of grace, a grant determined according to the following formula, namely, a grant equal to 75 per cent of the sum determined by taking that percentage of the general tax levy for municipal and school purposes-but excluding business taxes-which is equal to the percentage which total federal property assessments bear to total taxable assessments in the municipality, less four per cent.
The grant is to be equal to 75 per cent, rather than 100 per cent, of the sum determined by the above formula, for two reasons:
(a)	to reflect in some degree the fact mentioned above that benefits do accrue to the municipality from the presence of federal property within its limits; and
(b)	to take into account the further fact that there is always in any municipality a

proportion of other than federal property which is granted exemption from municipal tax.
In this formula the term "federal property" is taken to mean all federal properties, except such types as parks, harbours and more or less self-contained defence establishments and property owned by crown corporations or agencies. I am presenting a detailed schedule of the excluded categories which, with the permission of the house, I would like to have tabled and printed as an appendix to this statement. Certain of these excluded categories may, however, be included in the calculations for any particular municipality if such municipality can demonstrate that special conditions exist which warrant such inclusion.	,
It will be noted that while school taxes are taken into account in determining the amount of a grant, the total amount will be paid to the municipal corporation, which will have the responsibility of applying the amount of such grant in the best interests of all taxpayers in the municipality. It is clear, of course, that any contribution to the cost of any local service eases the burden on taxpayers generally for the total cost of their local services.
Perhaps I might now be permitted to give an illustration of how the formula would work out in the case of a hypothetical municipality. Take a municipality which has total tax assessments of $100 million. Using the same assessment practice, the total assessment of federal properties would amount to $10 million, or 10 per cent of the total. The municipal tax levy for ordinary and school purposes is $4 million. Our first step is to deduct the national average of federal property assessments to total municipal assessments, assumed at 4 per cent, from the figure of 10 per cent, which represents the corresponding figure for the municipality in question, leaving a net of six per cent. Applying this percentage, six per cent, to the total tax levy of $4 million, we arrive at the figure of $240,000. The grant payable in the case of this municipality would therefore be 75 per cent of this sum, namely, $180,000.
It will thus be seen that under the program which we are now prepared to recommend, the federal government intends to assume a proportionate share of the cost of maintaining ordinary municipal services in any municipality where the concentration of federal property is in excess of the national average. In return, the federal government will seek treatment in the matter of municipal services not less favourable than that accorded to ordinary taxpayers.

Crown Properties
It is proposed, in addition, to pay in future to any municipality in receipt of this type of grant a further temporary adjustment grant whenever the crown acquires a new piece of property in that municipality. This grant will ensure that the municipality will receive full taxes for the year in which the property is acquired, either from the vendor or from the government, depending on the sales agreement, plus full taxes in the succeeding year, and one half of taxes in the next following year. At the end of this period the assessed value of such property will be included in the total of federal assessment of the municipality-with a commensurate effect on the regular grant.
For any municipality where no regular grant is made because total federal property in that municipality is below the national average, the government proposes in future to pay, in respect of any piece of property acquired by the crown, full taxes for the year of acquisition in the same way as above, plus full taxes for the succeeding year and in each of the next three years grants of respectively 75 per cent, 50 per cent and 25 per cent of the full taxes. At the end of this five-year period no further grants will be paid. These temporary grants are intended to permit the municipalities to adjust themselves to the loss of specific tax revenue upon the acquisition of property by the crown.
We will also propose the payment as soon as possible of all proper arrears and charges for local improvements against federal real property in any municipality, and the payment of all local improvement charges as they occur in the future.
In addition it is the intention of the government to pay for all charges for water received at government buildings on a meter basis.
Finally, I wish to say a word about the position of property held by crown corporations. With respect to such property the situation is complicated, but in general the policy of the government will be to authorize its crown corporations to work out fair and equitable agreements with the municipalities in which their properties are situated.
In the case of residential housing property owned or managed by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, there are already agreements with municipalities providing for payments in lieu of taxes. Because agreements between Wartime Housing Limited and the municipalities in relation to war workers' houses provided for payments in lieu of taxes which were considered insufficient, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply on July 22, 1946, indicated that these agreements could

be renegotiated with the corporation, with corresponding increases in rents to be paid by individuals to meet the adjusted payments in lieu of taxes. Most agreements of this kind have now been renegotiated, and the balance can be renegotiated if the municipalities so desire. In regard to housing properties completed since 1947 and under current programs, payments in lieu of taxes are being made in accordance with agreements negotiated with the municipalities which are believed to be equitable and will not be renegotiated.
In the case of the government-owned railways operated by the Canadian National Railways, agreements have been entered into with the cities of Halifax and Saint John for the payment of reasonable amounts in lieu of taxes. I understand that the Canadian National Railways will endeavour to work out similar arrangements with other municipalities through which the government-owned railway runs.
In general, as I have indicated, the policy will be to have crown corporations work out arrangements with municipalities which are fair and equitable under all circumstances.
It should be clear from what I have said that the government intends to pursue policies in respect to its federal real property which will assure fair and equitable compensation to those municipalities which have a genuine burden as the result of the presence of federal property within their boundaries, and will assure the payment of legitimate costs as they occur in connection with its properties.
The government proposes to make immediate arrangements to have its property assessed by its agents for the purpose of determining the grants to be paid. Preliminary information indicates that, in a number of cases at least, local assessments of federal property are considerably inflated. It should be borne in mind that such assessments have been made without contest or rebuttal by the federal government, because hitherto the assessment of federal property has been a matter of academic interest only.
While the procedure of assessment will probably require a couple of years to complete, it is proposed to institute the program I have outlined as of the 1st of January, 1950. Actual payments in some cases may be delayed, but they will be made retroactive. For obvious reasons it will not be possible to institute the system of grants for those municipalities having within their limits federal properties to an extent near the assumed national average of four per cent until the actual certification of the figures has been

completed. However, for those municipalities which, according to our rough preliminary figures, would seem to be clearly within the ambit of the new scheme, we propose, if our recommendations are accepted by parliament, to commence payments as soon after January 1, 1950, as possible, withholding 25 per cent until the final determination of figures has been completed. Adjustments will be made retroactively.
Figures now available would indicate that there are something over one hundred municipalities where there is a concentration of federal property in excess of the national average. I hesitate at this time to make any estimate of what the total annual cost of the entire program will probably amount to but I believe it is likely to be in the vicinity of $5 million.
This new program will supersede any existing arrangements with certain municipalities, such as those which formerly existed with the city of Ottawa. This city, the capital of the dominion, is not only the most outstanding case amongst the municipalities affected by a substantial concentration of federal property, but the situation is rather more complicated here, because of the proposed development of the national capital plan. This has, I am afraid, led to some confusion, and we think it important to a clear understanding of the proposals we are making, and to a satisfactory solution of our relationships with the city, that it be clearly recognized that in the case of the city of Ottawa there are two distinct and separate problems: first, the problem arising from the presence of a large amount of tax-exempt federal property within the city limits; and second, the financial problem which may be faced by the city in fulfilling its part in its own development as the national capital of Canada, as envisaged in the Greber report.
We fear that confusion in regard to these two problems has made them seem a lot more difficult and complicated than they really are. The discussion of relative participations in some new capital planning project has been complicated by arguments based on inadequate compensation for abnormal concentration of federal property, and vice versa. At times also statements have been made which appear to overemphasize the burdens placed upon the city by the presence of federal property or fail to take into account the contribution which the federal government is already making. Perhaps it is well that all hon. members should first be clear about this latter point. At the present time the federal government does its own policing, paves and maintains a good part of Wellington street, the federal district highways, Clemow avenue and two bridges over the Ottawa river, with
Crown Properties
the approaches thereto; maintains the federal district parks system, including a few of the city's own parks; collects and disposes of garbage from its own buildings; pays for all the water it uses at the fair rate of 20-82 cents per thousand gallons, and pays to the city an annual grant of $300,000 in lieu of taxes. On the other hand, the city supplies light and water for the parks and parkways within the city limits to which I have referred.
I wish now to outline the new arrangements which we are proposing. In regard to Ottawa's first problem arising from concentration of federal property, the government believes that the city should be treated in this respect in exactly the same way as a great many other municipalities which are confronted with the same problem in greater or less degree. In other words, if parliament approves the general program of grants I have outlined, the city of Ottawa will receive as from January 1 next a grant in lieu of taxes determined on the basis of the same formula as that applicable to all other municipalities. However, the arrangement which has been in effect in the past lapsed on June 30 last, and it is therefore necessary to decide on a grant to the city for the rest of the current year. I am happy now to announce that the government has decided to recommend payment to Ottawa of an interim grant of $250,000 to cover this six-months period. For the present it is not proposed to disturb the existing arrangement whereby the government now provides certain services for itself in Ottawa, as I have indicated. However, in accordance with our intention of seeking equal treatment in future in the matter of municipal services, these arrangements will be reviewed with the municipality when the new plan of regular grants in lieu of municipal taxes comes into effect.
Having disposed of this first problem in the way suggested, we hope it will now be possible to deal with the second problem separately and on its own merits. This second problem arises, as I have already indicated, from the necessity of financing the development of the national capital. For some years past, as the house is aware, members of the federal district commission and others who are members of the national capital planning committee, including a number of experts, have been working on a plan for the development of the capital. A master plan is being prepared setting out on broad lines the developments which should be followed from year to year by the different authorities and organizations having to do with the development of the capital.
From the very outset it has been recognized that the implementation of any master plan

Crown Properties
befitting the requirements of a national capital would involve developments of a character beyond the municipal improvements ordinarily required in other cities. This was foreshadowed in the report, dated August 1, 1944, of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons appointed to review the special problems arising out of the location of the seat of government in the city of Ottawa. The resolution which was passed by this house in June, 1948, explicitly recognized that fact and its corollary that "the development of a national capital is at least in part a national responsibility." For that reason the resolution went on to recommend the creation of a special account in the consolidated revenue fund, to be known as the national capital fund, to which appropriations would be made annually by parliament over a period of years of the amounts required from time to time to meet the costs of such projects as might be recommended by the federal district commission and approved by the governor in council for the development of the national capital and the surrounding area in accordance with the developing master plan. As hon. members are aware, the sum of $2J million was voted to be set aside in that national capital fund last year, and a similar item is included in the estimates for the current fiscal year.
On behalf of the government, therefore, I now wish to make it clear that we are prepared to see appropriate assistance given on the recommendation of the commission in the case of those individual projects which are considered essential in the development of the national capital plan, and yet would not be undertaken, at least not in the same form or to the same extent or at as early a date, if Ottawa were not the capital of our country and it were not necessary to have regard to the future development of the country as well as of the municipality. This would include, for example, part of the extra cost that might be necessary to make a new city hall comply with the architectural requirements of the national capital plan if the city should eventually decide to place it in a location where such additional standards would be required. Another example would include certain features of the Gore and Storrie report on sewage and water supply, and new Sussex street bridges over the Rideau river to complete the gap in the eastern end of the driveway system.
The federal district commission has power to discuss with the city participation in any one of these individual projects or developments. Any project will be considered on its own merits and on the degree of its

relationship to the city as an ordinary municipality or to the national capital, as the case may be.
Furthermore, the government proposes, in addition to the regular grant to the city, to make additional funds available to the federal district commission to cover additional expense which it may be necessary for the city to incur in co-operation and agreement with the commission in carrying out its obligations under provincial planning statutes, such as zoning and laying out on the ground by surveys the necessary features of the national capital plan. The amount of funds so made available will not be a fixed grant, but it is likely to vary to some extent from time to time, depending on the projects likely to be undertaken during the period in question.
It is the hope of the government that by keeping our consideration of this national capital development problem separate and distinct from the other general problem to which I referred in the early part of my remarks, we shall be able to remove the confusions and misunderstandings that may have existed in the past and secure the effective co-operation of the city authorities in promoting the growth and development of this beautiful city in its role of the national capital.
In conclusion, may I say that we would propose to ask for parliamentary approval of the interim grant to Ottawa and the initiation of the program for the whole of Canada by a special estimates item to be introduced at this session of parliament. I believe only a modest appropriation of funds at this session, over and above the amount of the interim grant to Ottawa, will be necessary to make possible the setting up of the necessary establishment in the Department of Finance, work out details of procedure, begin the job of assessments of federal property and provide for such initial grants as may have to be made before the close of the present fiscal year. At the next session it would be our intention to introduce a bill to provide permanent statutory authorization of the program as a whole. (Schedule of excluded categories follows:)

Detailed Schedule of Categories Excluded From the Definition of Federal Property
Total federal property shall mean all federal property within municipal boundaries in organized territory, except:
(1)	All military, naval and air force establishments which are self-contained or substantially so.
(2)	AH harbours, canals and other lands held in connection with the federal government's responsibility for navigable waters.
(3)	All lands held in connection with land conservation, irrigation, rehabilitation and forestation.

<4) All penitentiaries and D.V.A. hospitals where they are outside of urban municipal boundaries and/or self-contained or substantially so.
(5)	All parks and parklands and historical sites and other improvements of a like nature.
(6)	All property held by crown corporations or agencies.
(7)	Canadian government-owned railways.
(8)	Property of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Any of the above types of property in classifications 1 to 4 inclusive may be included in whole or in part for the purpose of determining the principal grant if in the opinion of the minister a municipality has demonstrated a good case for its inclusion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: NATIONAL ART GALLERY
speechtext:
1.	The government has given consideration to the question of a new building for the National Art Gallery of Canada and has authorized the board of trustees to proceed with the necessary preliminary inquiries regarding the most suitable type of construction.
2.	Mr. Southam has resigned as chairman of the board of trustees, but he remains a member of the board.
3.	On the occasion of Mr. Southam's resignation Mr. Mackenzie King, who was then prime minister, expressed to Mr. Southam, in a letter dated January 29, 1948, the appreciation of the government for the fine services which he had rendered. A copy of this letter appears below. It gives me much pleasure now to add my thanks and appreciation for what Mr. Southam has done and for the support which he continues to give to the national gallery.
Office of the Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa, January 29, 1948
H. S. Southam, Esq.,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Southam:
The government has acceded reluctantly to your request to be relieved of the responsibilities of the chairmanship of the board of trustees of the national gallery. I should, however, not like the occasion to pass without expression, on behalf of the government, a word of appreciation of the fine national service you have rendered in the nineteen-years you have been chairman.
During that period the national gallery has made a steadily growing contribution to the cultural life of our country, and has become in increasing measure, not merely a repository of the art treasures of the nation, but also a centre of artistic inspiration. Under your chairmanship the board of trustees have guided and fostered this development and laid enduring foundations for the future of the national gallery.
It is a source of satisfaction to the government that you are to remain as a member of the board, in which capacity we know you will continue to render valuable service to the national gallery and to the appreciation of the arts in the country at large.
With kind personal regards,
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King

speakeroldname: Hon. Siuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 144, to amend the Combines Investigation Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving second reading I shall follow the usual practice of discussing only the principles of the bill. Those principles are two. The first is that of withdrawing from corporate accused in prosecutions under the act the option it now has of choosing whether it shall be tried by a jury or without a jury. The second is that in prosecutions under this act there shall be a rebuttable presumption that an employee acting in connection with his employer's business has authority so to act, and a rebuttable presumption that relevant documents in the business files of those involved in an alleged combine are authentic records from which a court or a jury may properly draw any reasonable inferences.
To begin with, may I say that the entire contents of this bill are made up of recommendations of the combines investigation administration, which have been approved by the government.
I shall deal with the principles of the bill in the order in which I stated them.
Under the present law, offences under the combines act and under section 498 of the Criminal Code can be tried only by a superior court judge with or without a jury, at the option of the accused. The proposed amendment provides that, not in the case of an individual but only in the case of a company, the company shall be tried by a supreme court judge without a jury, and shall not have the option of being tried with a jury. After the adoption of this amendment an individual, of course, can still elect jury or non-jury trial at his pleasure.
Jury trials are singularly inappropriate for the trial of combines cases, because of the complexity and volume of the evidence and the length of time required to present these cases to the courts. In that connection I might cite two fairly typical cases. First is Rex v. Container Materials Limited et al., where the number of pages of transcript was 5,111, the number of exhibits tendered 323, and the length of trial in days, 39. The second is Rex v. Imperial Tobacco Company of Canada and others, in which the number of pages of transcript was 8,798, the number of exhibits tendered 1,127, and the length of trial in days 56.
In these cases the accused invariably are companies or incorporated business firms or officials of such companies or firms or of trade

associations made up of a number of these Arms acting in an industry. Of necessity the evidence is largely documentary; and if a dozen or more companies and individuals are indicted, as is usually the case, very close study must be given to their corporate interrelationship one with the other and to the usually involved arrangements into which they enter in order, as alleged, to control prices or otherwise limit competition. Activities of all the accused and their principal employees must be traced in evidence over a considerable period, in some cases over many years, and also in many related aspects.
The presentation of evidence drawn from many different sources and relating to many different matters is extremely difficult in any jury trial, as I think any legal member of this house will agree; and it imposes a heavy burden upon the presiding judge and upon counsel in the submission of the evidence to the jury. An equally heavy burden-in my own view a greater one, as a matter of fact- is placed upon the jurymen, who in almost all cases are laymen in relation to the problems with which the case deals, in analysing and weighing the intricate evidence presented during the trial, which usually occupies several weeks, and ultimately arriving at a conclusion with respect to the involved agreements, arrangements and transactions which form the substance of the charge.
Non-jury trial of charges of this sort permits a much more orderly and concise presentation of evidence to the court and a better-ordered arrangement of the facts brought out in the documentary and other evidence. All documents do not have to be read aloud, as must be done in a jury trial; and when you have exhibits running into the thousands you can see what a tremendous burden is imposed upon counsel on both sides of the case in retaining the interest of a jury throughout the reading aloud of documents. If a judge is trying the case without a jury, he may dispense with the full reading of lengthy records of which only a few passages may be either important or relevant. The possibility of mistrial through death or illness of a juror in cases the trial of which extends over a long period, such as those I have mentioned, or through procedural errors or through misdirection by the trial judge, is avoided or reduced. The length and expense of the trial, both for the crown and for the accused, is also reduced.
Admittedly in some cases two trials may be necessary after this amendment passes, one for the companies and for the individuals who may elect non-jury trial, and one for those individuals who may choose to elect trial by jury. But such a split trial can occur even
Combines Investigation Act under the existing legislation. In both the A.B.C. plumbing case in 1931 and the tobacco case in 1941 there were split trials under the present legislation, one trial for those electing a jury and one for those electing nonjury.
In this connection I should like to draw a clear distinction between the principle of withdrawing the privilege of jury trial from a corporation, as we are proposing to do here, and that of withdrawing a jury trial from an individual, which we are not proposing to do. The arguments for a non-jury trial in combines cases could apply, perhaps not to the same extent but to some extent, to trials of individuals as well as trials of corporations, but we are not proposing to withdraw the right of an individual to trial by a jury of his peers, because of the strong British and Canadian tradition in favour of that principle.
We have it in mind that a distinction can be made between a natural person, who must appear in court himself to answer charges and is subject to both fine and imprisonment, and an artificial person such as a corporation, which appears in court only through counsel, and cannot, of course, be penalized by imprisonment. If the rights of the corporation are otherwise adequately protected, there is no unfairness in limiting the trial to a judge without a jury. The prime consideration, we submit, must be the ends of justice and the interests of the public. The public advantages in connection with this matter are many, and we affirm that the corporation is under no undue hardship by reason of the limitation which we propose.

speechtext: Will the minister permit a question at this point? He pointed to the distinction between a natural person and an artificial person. Is there any provision in either Great Britain or the United States for the denial to an artificial person of trial by jury?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I presume my hon. friend's question is intended to be relevant to the matter we are discussing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman spoke of the British tradition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
In Great Britain, as I understand it, an organization of the type which we have under the Combines Investigation Act has only recently been set up. Last spring the head of that body visited Canada to find out how we were carrying on under our act. The United Kingdom did not propose even to pass an act creating criminal offences until the matter had received careful con-
45781- 1094

Combines Investigation Act sideration. I am sure therefore that the question of withholding from a corporate accused the privilege of being tried by a jury has not arisen in that country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: They proceed under the criminal law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I would not want my hon. friend to leave the implication by his question that we are suggesting a change in anything other than the prosecutions under this act or the related section of the Criminal Code. It merely applies to such proceedings. If the hon. member followed my remarks carefully, he must have seen that we were basing the reason for this change upon the nature of this particular type of prosecution.
As I was saying, in Great Britain they have not yet arrived at the point of passing criminal legislation which would correspond to our Combines Investigation Act. The question of their withdrawing this privilege, therefore, from a corporate accused has not yet arisen. I cannot answer my hon. friend's question relating to the United States practice, but in any event their approach to this whole matter is considerably different from our own, as I think he is well aware.
The second principle has to do with the establishment of the rebuttable presumptions to which I have already referred. The necessity for introducing amending legislation at this time, as I am sure all members are aware, has arisen by reason of the uncertainty in the law resulting from the decision of the Ontario court of appeal in February, 1949, in the dental supplies case. The problem created by this decision has been carefully studied, first of all, by the leading counsel in that case, and then by the legal advisers of the Department of Justice, as well as the combines investigation branch of that department. Section 3 of the proposed bill represents the results of that study.
Perhaps some considerable amount of light will be shed upon the provisions we have before us for consideration if I make some reference to the dental supplies judgment. The prosecution of members of the Canadian Dental Trade Association was undertaken by the Attorney General of Canada after a report had been made by the commissioner alleging that a combine existed amongst the various members of the association, which included both manufacturers and dealers. Eighteen corporations with head offices in various parts of Canada were tried at Toronto in March, 1948. At the end of the crown's case, the trial judge acquitted the accused, upon the ground that some five hundred documents presented as evidence during the three weeks of trial had not been sufficiently authenticated. This judgment was confirmed by the
fMr. Garson.]
unanimous judgment of the court of appeal on February 28, 1949. The argument on appeal was heard in the fall of 1948, the latter part of September and October, but the judgment was reserved and was not delivered until 1949.	.
The documents on which the crown based its case had been introduced in evidence on proof that they came from the business offices of the accused companies and that, coming from those offices, they had evidentiary value. Crown counsel argued that the court should apply to the companies the principle, long established in conspiracy trials, that documents and other things found in the possession of the accused are evidence against him. The crown claimed that the contents of these documents fully established the interest of the companies in the alleged illegal agreements, and also established the authority of the officers and employees to enter into those agreements on behalf of their respective companies. The trial judge, although at the beginning of the trial he had admitted these documents in evidence, rejected the crown's argument and refused to let the documents go to the jury, on the ground that they had no probative value without further proof.
When the case came before the court of appeal, the court, in a unanimous decision delivered by the chief justice, confirmed the trial court judgment and established the principle that where companies are accused, the criminal acts which are charged against them must be brought home to the companies by more direct evidence than the filing of these seized documents. In this connection the chief justice stated:
The proof required, however, in the case of a company, differs somewhat from that required in the case of an individual. If the act relied on is that of an officer, servant or agent of the company, there must be evidence that he had authority from the company to perform the act. Mere possession of a document by a company, in the sense that the document was on its premises, and even in the company's files, may not, without more, afford ground for an inference that its contents had come to the knowledge of its board of directors, or of someone having authority from, the company to deal with the matters to which the document relates.
At a later point in his judgment his lordship said:
There is, however, one objection common to all the letters. There is no evidence that the writing of any of them was authorized by any of the accused companies, nor is there evidence that anyone having authority to bind the company had any knowledge of the sending of any of the letters or of their receipt or of their contents.
Sir, most combines cases involve combination or conspiracy among a large number of companies, and usually over a considerable period of years. The basic agreement between the companies, if it exists, and if illegal, is normally secret and not contained in any

formal documents. Ordinarily its existence, its nature and its effect must be deduced from the acts of company officials recorded in a vast amount of correspondence, memoranda, and other documents found on the files of the companies and their associates. Oral evidence of these facts is often not available or singularly unreliable. It requires no great amount of imagination to realize that, when you are seizing documents in the possession of the corporate accused, the securing of corroborative oral testimony from the officials or employees of the accused corporation is in the nature of things a difficult matter.
If no amendment such as we now propose in this instance were made, the crown, in most combines cases, would be required to prove by oral evidence the authority of company officials to bind their company, and in effect we would be required, directly or indirectly, to supply oral proof of virtually all the facts which are set forth in the documents.
In the trial of offences in conspiracy cases, this so-called possessory principle has been frequently applied. Its application in a case of this sort means that these incriminating documents would, without oral proof, have such probative force as the jury or the judge might be disposed to give to them. One of the effects of the decision in the dental supplies cases is that of making a distinction between individuals accused and corporations accused with regard to the possessory basis of proof.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That was not a new principle. It was not enunciated for the first time in that case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, I am stating that it was enunciated in that case, and no more than that. When my hon. friend speaks he can show that it was not enunciated for the first time in that case.
Another practical result of the dental judgment is that if this amendment is not enacted the crown will have to prove by oral evidence the authority of company officials to bind their respective companies. This means that positive proof would have to be given by word of mouth, by having witnesses of virtually all the facts which, under the possessory rule in the case of individuals, can be inferred from mere possession.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is what made me wonder why the minister did not appeal the judgment. I think it is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks that the judgment is wrong, I hope he will support this amendment.

different principle altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
If witnesses from the companies must be available to prove authority, they will usually be capable of proving by direct oral evidence the writing of the documents and the truth of the facts stated in them. Thus the dental judgment gravely limits the application of the possessory principle, and tends to establish one principle for companies which are accused and another principle for individual persons who are accused.
In considering this amendment one of the facts which must be realized is that these combines prosecutions are not by any means ordinary run-of-mine pieces of litigation. Because of the special nature and the extraordinary complexity of combines cases, in all instances except the most extremely simple ones an unnecessarily heavy burden is placed upon the crown by the decision in the dental supplies case.
The problem which the crown faces in a typical combines prosecution can be illustrated by the following paragraph from the memorandum of fact and law submitted by the crown to the court of appeal in the dental supplies case. This is an extract from our factum in that case:
24. In this case counsel for the crown were instructed that there were over 2,000 relevant documents in the possession of the accused extending over a period of eighteen years. The proving of all these documents by proof of handwriting or other execution was impossible in practice, and any substantial attempt to do so would have taken months of trial, required the attendance of witnesses from all parts of Canada and abroad and would have left unproven in that way, documents vital to the case.
That is to say, it would take months; it would involve the bringing of witnesses from all over Canada and abroad. Even then there would be vital documents which it would be impossible to prove by oral evidence because oral evidence in relation to them does not exist; although, if they had been tendered in respect of an individual case or a natural person, the mere fact that they had been taken from the possession of the accused would admit them as evidence for whatever probative value the jury or the judge might think they should have.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, there is one thing I should like to emphasize strongly. We are not suggesting for a minute that the presumption which the tendering of these seized documents establishes against the accused is an irrebuttable and conclusive presumption. All we are saying is that we put them in for whatever value the court chooses to give to them, and the accused, if they be innocent, can then come forward with cogent evidence to the contrary and rebut the presumption which has been raised by the admission of these documents.

I hold in my hand the report on some leading cases of law relating to this possessory principle. I do not think I shall detain the house with them. Perhaps it would be preferable if I let the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) develop the legal proposition to which he referred a few minutes ago, and if necessary I can reply to him at the close of the debate.
But this much should be said. I think the hon. member will agree with me that, so far as natural persons are concerned, the possessory principle is well established. So far as the principle applies to the corporate accused, we have successfully invoked it in several of the prosecutions, in order to establish a case. The cases of Rex v. Simington and Rex v. Container Materials Limited, to give two of them, are in point.
One of the reasons this proposed change in the legislation is necessary is that it has been the experience of the combines investigation administration that where agreements, illegal under the Combines Investigation Act, are entered into, it is seldom indeed that the board of directors of an accused company goes to the trouble of formally authorizing the entering into of that agreement by their concern. It is also seldom that any person in an official capacity in a company does so. And if it be necessary in these cases, where the documents seized from a corporate accused, when they are pieced together in a very large jigsaw puzzle-if that is the appropriate figure of speech-show the establishment of the agreement, that we then have to show that the board of directors authorized it, or that the general manager authorized the agreement, I should think there would be very few occasions indeed where it would ever be possible to secure a conviction.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What officers does the minister think could give such authorization? Would a sales manager be sufficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think there is any statement as to what particular officers could do so. The point, in reply to my hon. friend's interjection, is that the onus is upon the crown to show that the acts complained of were authorized by some person who had authority.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: It is a normal onus, in any case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is a normal onus in most cases where the agreements you are attempting to prove are legal ones upon which a company may be suing or depending to establish a defence. But where an agreement is an illegal one, a prudent company does not as a rule delegate to its responsible officers, or its people with authority, the forming of illegal agreement.


I think it might be of service,, and shed some light upon the matter, if I were to refer to some of the typical documents which have to be put in evidence in cases of this kind. Almost all evidence in a typical combines prosecution consists of informal documents such as minutes, memoranda and some letters. Only very rarely is the case based, either in whole or in part, upon any formal contracts or agreements between the parties. Usually the informal documentary evidence either specifically describes the agreements or contains statements which clearly warrant the inference that agreements were entered into.
Most of the evidence submitted consists of documents coming from the possession of or otherwise proved as originating from someone who has participated in the alleged combine. Again, the documents almost always come from members-usually incorporated companies-of the combines who are actually accused. They may thus come from the accused companies or firms, from their branches, or from the possession of officials of such companies or of such firms.
Another important body of evidence is usually found in the possession of the secretary of the trade association to which the accused belonged-a trade association which in some cases the crown alleges was formed for the purpose of achieving an illegal agreement of the firms in it. Occasionally evidence may be found in the files of companies which were originally in the combine but which have now discontinued business or have been taken over by accused companies.
As I have already indicated, documents adduced as necessary evidence sometimes number several thousand. In most cases, however, the most essential or primary evidence may be only a selection of some three or four hundred documents out of the thousands. These usually consist of memoranda purporting to record meetings at which agreements have been made or implemented, and also selected key letters which record or refer to arrangements between the accused. Usually much of such principal evidence is found in the possession of the trade association secretary, although in some cases, where the secretary has carefully avoided keeping incriminating evidence, the documents may be found scattered in the files of the various accused or their associates. Also usually essential are agreed price lists or agreed lists of customers which have been distributed among the members of the alleged combine.
The remaining documentary evidence in a typical case consists of minor memoranda of meetings, inter-office memoranda and a large

body of miscellaneous letters. This remaining evidence is usually of a supplementary nature illustrating or corroborating the essential agreements, showing how they have been carried out through the relevant period and showing the participation of the various accused corporations.

It is now necessary for every hon. member of this house to ask himself whether the proposed amendments are necessary; whether they are adequate, and whether they will have any appreciable effect if the government continues to assert its right to disregard the laws passed by the parliament of Canada. Members of this house are not here merely for the purpose of hearing bills read and registering their votes. Their action here is intended to have some effect. More than that, the time has come for every hon. member to realize that parliament, not the government, is the supreme authority.
Combines Investigation Act Under our parliamentary system the government is merely the administrative body chosen from the members of the house by the leader of the government and nominated by the representative of His Majesty the King to form a government. That government at all times is responsible to the house. That government at all times must answer to the house. That government at all times is duty bound to observe in the strictest details the provisions which the parliament of Canada has seen fit to enact as the laws of this country.

It is for that reason that I propose to introduce an amendment to this motion before the conclusion of my remarks.
Members of this house should know exactly what has taken place. The trouble is that we have had at least two different explanations for the government's action in not dealing with the report of the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act, which had so much to do with the recent resignation of that experienced official. It will be most helpful to the members of this house if they know what has been under discussion, because the explanations that have been given leave this house in great uncertainty as to what actually took place.
I submit that the motion to give this bill second reading now brings directly in issue in this house the circumstances which have brought the administration of the Combines Investigation Act so prominently to the attention of the people of Canada within these past few days.
In considering what changes, if any, should be made in the Combines Investigation Act, and in determining the procedure which should be followed in deciding what changes should be made, we must of necessity review the position taken by the government in regard to its responsibilities under the act. It is not enough that we examine the cold words of the act. It is also necessary that we examine the attitude of the government toward the enforcement of it, so that we may

know how effective any amendment will be, or what further steps should be taken to prevent even this government from defying the law as passed by the parliament of Canada.
Any consideration of the act at this time would be meaningless unless the circumstances leading to the resignation of Mr. F. A. McGregor are carefully examined in every essential detail. A fundamentally important issue is raised by the action of the government following the delivery of Mr. McGregor's report which recommended the prosecution of a number of milling companies for what the commissioner regarded as breaches of the act. It does not seem to me that the question whether there was or was not a breach of the Combines Investigation Act, in the particular case to which I have referred, is really the fundamentally important issue before the house at the present time. The sequence of events is not disputed.
According to Mr. McGregor, the investigation of the alleged combine in the milling industry was started with the knowledge and approval of Mr. Ilsley, who was then minister of justice. So far as I am aware, that statement has not been challenged. If it is correct, then the investigation proceeded with the knowledge and approval of the minister to whom the commissioner is directly answerable. It is clear that the Department of Justice must have been aware at all times that the investigation was proceeding and approved what was being done so far as the conduct of the investigation was concerned.
Mr. McGregor completed his investigation and made his report to the Minister of Justice on December 29, 1948. Section 27 of the Combines Investigation Act leaves no doubt whatever as to what must then be done. It is not optional; it is mandatory. Subsection 5 of section 27 reads as follows:
Any report of the commissioner or a special commissioner, other than an interim report or a report of a preliminary inquiry under section 13 of this act, shall within fifteen days after its receipt by the minister be made public, unless the commissioner states in writing to the minister that he believes the public interest would be better served by withholding publication, in which case the minister may decide whether the report, either in whole or in part, shall be made public.
There is no authority given to the minister to withhold publication of a report after fifteen days have elapsed unless the commissioner has expressed in writing to the minister his opinion that the interests of the public will best be served by withholding publication of it. Therefore, as of January 13 of this year, the Minister of Justice was in default as to a mandatory requirement of a law enacted by this parliament.

There may be a tendency on the part of some hon. members to think that the question of publication is a relatively unimportant detail. There may be a tendency on the part of some people to regard publication as merely a formality, and to think that the violation by the Minister of Justice of a law passed by this parliament, such violation being with the approval and decision of the government, is in itself a relatively unimportant matter. This is not the opinion that has been held by others; it is not the opinion that was held by the gentleman who preceded the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and whose opinions are so frequently cited with approval by members of the government. Publication was regarded as extremely important, and at all times it was emphasized that the publication of such reports was for the purpose of informing the public as to what had taken place, and of bringing to public attention those things which, by publication itself, might tend to prevent a repetition of the same events.

He advanced it without argument and more or less, as I saw it, as a question, without pressing too strongly the citation to which he referred. I think one way to find out whether or not what took place from the discussion on November 7 could be referred to would be to reduce the situation to its ultimate conclusion. Citation 345 in Beauchesne's third edition states:
The ancient doctrine that the redress of grievances should be considered before the grant of supplies is maintained in the House of Commons of Canada by the provision of standing order 49 that the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair can be amended: and the amendments need not be relevant but may relate to every question connected with public administration.
Then a little later on it says this:
Members may discuss various matters on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair without any amendment being proposed; but once debate is stopped on one matter and another matter intervenes, members cannot again discuss the former.
In the event that a minister of the crown did not desire a discussion to take place on a matter of interest to the people of Canada,
Combines Investigation Act all he would have to do would be to rise in his place in the house when the motion was made that the Speaker do now leave the chair, and have an amendment and a subamendment proposed. Yes; once there is a motion, an amendment and a subamendment, there can be no further subamendment. When a subamendment is moved, a person who does not wish to have a discussion of any subject-and it could come from this side as well as the other-would simply rise in his place and for a moment make an explanation, and then he would have somebody immediately follow him, dealing with some other subject. That would end for that session any further discussion.
This would lead to a position wherein parliament would indeed be throttled and its voice be silenced at the wish of one or two members in the house. I submit that the very fact that that would be the result indicates why it is there are no authorities I can find that will support the view that, when a matter is merely raised and no motion or amendment is based thereupon, the fact that something is referred to denies further discussion.
During the noon recess I looked up the first reference to be found in May in this matter.
It is to be found in Commons Journals, volume 113, 1857 and 1858, page 65. This motion arose under the following circumstances: There was a controversy at the time regarding foreign affairs, in which the government of the day was desirous of not having any discussion. A motion was made, and a bill to meet the particular facts of the case was introduced. There had been a discussion of the subject during the preceding week, as will be seen in British Hansard for February 11, 12 and 13. On February 19 a motion was made by the government, and an amendment moved covering matters that had been discussed but not decided upon during the preceding week. The question being proposed, no exception was taken to it, and it was an amendment that had the result of defeating the then government. That is how serious the amendment was on that occasion. Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone would suggest that casual reference to a subject arising during the course of the debate on the address, or the debate on the budget, or the debate on the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair, would preclude further discussion. It is always a question of substance. Has there been a substantive debate on the matter, or has there not been such a debate? Hon. members will realize it has frequently happened in this house-I think the argument of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is a good reminder- that there have been repetitious debates on the same matter. Mr. Speaker, the rule to which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has referred itself answers the argument whether or not this matter has been disposed of in such a way as to preclude further debate on the same subject. The relevant citation reads:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members that they cannot revive a debate already concluded; and it would be little use in preventing the same question from being offered twice in the same session, if, without being offered, its merits might be discussed again) and again.
In the first place, may I point out that no question has been presented to this house in regard to the Combines Investigation Act or the subject matter of the statement introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce last Monday on the motion to go into supply. In the second place, there was no debate on

the Combines Investigation Act, the circumstances related to Mr. McGregor's resignation, the violation of this law by the government, or any related subject, which was actually concluded.
The reason for this rule is so obvious that it needs little elaboration. If the members of this house deal with a motion which brings before the house arguments on both sides and then make their decision, it must certainly seem to be, not only a wholesome restraint but a very common-sense limitation upon the time to be taken in a particular debate to say that that same debate must not be revived. This debate was not on the Combines Investigation Act, on the administration of that act, or on the breach of the law by the government.
There was a motion to go into supply. There was an amendment to that motion. Availing himself of the opportunity to use such a motion to introduce the subject-I do not question the fact that that practice is established-the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealt to a limited extent with a particular aspect of the problem now before the house. May I point out what the difficulty would be if a ruling were made that the debate is limited by what occurred on Monday. Reference was made to the Combines Investigation Act and to action taken under that act. Does this mean that we cannot discuss it at all? If so, the explanation of the Minister of Justice, and everything else that has been said, is out of order.
At what point does the knife fall? At what point does the iron curtain descend? Unless it is possible at the same time to say just how far this limitation goes, then the limitation extends over the whole field of discussion of the Combines Investigation Act. All that this house has had in regard to this matter is a statement, presented on a motion that had nothing directly to do with it, in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave his understanding of the action that had been taken, which incidentally is in conflict with the explanation given by the Minister of Justice.

The point that I now raise is that if any such ruling as this were made, not only would it be an easy device for effectively preventing debate on what might be regarded as a subject that the government did not wish to discuss; there would also be a never-never land created in which no one could tell exactly at what point the debate would be permitted to extend and where it might not.
The statement to which reference has been made was simply a limited statement as to

the broad point of view in regard to what had occurred. I fail to see how any hon. member of this house could possibly determine at what point he would be infringing upon the restriction suggested by citation 245 if it were ruled that what has taken place on the motion to go into supply can be regarded as a limitation upon further discussion of that subject although there was no conclusion.
Again I emphasize this point. The rule is that you cannot revive a debate already concluded, but no debate on any aspect of the Combines Investigation Act has been concluded, or upon the conduct of any minister or any official of this government. There is the provision that there shall not be a revival of a debate upon the same question. Subject is one thing; question is another. "Question" implies that there was an opportunity for the members to deal with the question before them. They did not have that opportunity in the motion before the house last Monday, and, therefore, within the actual wording of citation 245, I submit that nothing has occurred which limits full discussion of any aspect of what has already been mentioned in this house.

Mr. Speaker, before you rise to give your ruling may I draw your attention to a few facts which are not without importance.
In the first place, this is not a question of parliamentary procedure, because there is no standing order on the matter. This is purely a question of parliamentary practice. As there are no precedents that apply to this case, you will have to use your good sense, your experience and your sound judgment to give a ruling that will satisfy the mind of every one of my hon. colleagues.
The debate on the point of order has been on a high plane. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made a learned speech, but he spoke Greek, to me. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) made a scientific speech but he spoke Hebrew. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) was too technical, and he spoke either Latin or Armenian. I do not know which. We must approach the matter from the point of view of reason in order that the Chair may give a ruling that will serve not only for this occasion but for the future. The main thing is to know what is meant by a revival of debate. No one has defined it. It is up to you, Mr. Speaker, to say what is a revival of debate. How often, when points of order are debated, do I realize that hon. members take definitions for granted. There is no standing order to
Combines Investigation Act cover what is a revival of debate. We have no precedent, and yet we talk about it as if we all knew what it is. Please tell us in your ruling, Mr. Speaker, what is a revival of debate.
The second point is that none of the opposition members who have spoken have shown the relation that exists between a debate on the McGregor report and a debate on the amending bill. If there is no relation, then there is no revival of debate. If there is some relation there might be a revival of debate, or the McGregor incident might be considered as an interlude between the first and second readings of the bill. I should like any member of the opposition, or any other member of the house, to tell me what the relation is, if any, existing between the McGregor report and the debate on the second reading of the amendments to the combines legislation.
