speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
May I, at the outset, thank hon. members for the extended and helpful observations they have made on this important matter. I have allowed a full and unrestricted debate on the point of order because I realize it is a very important one, and I think the house is most anxious that I should have all the pertinent citations before me when giving my ruling.
After the order of the day has been read for the second reading of a bill or otherwise, the remarks of members must be "strictly relevant to the business under consideration." (Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, citation 140).
The "business under consideration" on the second reading of a bill is the principle of the bill. Members must accordingly confine themselves to a discussion of that principle and must refrain from introducing or referring to extraneous matters. (Bourinot, Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, page 509). The words which I am about to utter refer directly to this bill.
On the second reading of an amending bill -hon. members will notice that this is an amending bill-it is the principle of the amending bill, and not the principle of the act to be amended, which is the "business under consideration." The discussion must therefore relate exclusively to the principle of the amending bill. If, for example, a bill were introduced to amend a certain section of the Criminal Code of Canada, the discussion would have to relate to the principle of the particular amendment. It would be irregular to enter upon a general discussion of the Criminal Code as a whole. See Blackmore's Speakers' (Denison's and Brand's) Decisions, 1857-84, at page 70.
The principle of the present bill, an act to amend the Combines Investigation Act, is that it is desirable to facilitate the enforcement of that act by providing for the institution of proceedings by the Attorney General of Canada, by eliminating jury trials where corporations are charged with offences under the act, and by modifying and clarifying the applicable rules of evidence. The present discussion should accordingly relate exclusively to this principle. It is not in order to

discuss the principle of the Combines Investigation Act itself, or to discuss clauses of that act, or other matters, not clearly related to the principle of the amending bill.
It seems clear that a renewed general discussion of the McGregor report, a debate on which took place on November 7 on the motion to go into supply, is not in order on the motion for the second reading of this bill, because the discussion must relate exclusively to the principle of the amending bill.
Most of the discussion on the point of order has turned on citation 245, Beauchesne, third edition, which restates a passage from May's fourteenth edition, and reads as follows:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members that they cannot revive a debate already concluded; and it would be little use in preventing the same question from being offered twice in the same session if, without being offered, its merits might be discussed again and again.
I am of the opinion that this citation would not preclude all reference to matters dealt with during the earlier debate on the motion to go into supply so long as the reference can be shown to relate clearly to the principle of the amending bill now before the house. In reaching this conclusion I have also been conscious of the fact that the matter of the McGregor report was raised on the motion to go into supply as the result of a ministerial statement, and not by a private member raising a grievance or speaking in opposition to the motion. This being so it would seem inequitable to rule out of order all reference to the matters dealt with at that time.
On the other hand, it seems to me there are many aspects of the McGregor report which bear no relation to the bill before the house, and the discussion of which would not be in order on the motion for second reading. Nevertheless, in view of all the circumstances connected with the present debate, I think some reasonable leeway should be allowed. I refer to May, 14th edition, at page 497:
Debate on the stages of a bill should be confined to the bill, and should not be extended to a criticism of administration . . . but the Speaker remarked, when called upon to enforce this rule, that on many such occasions some licence was conceded to hon. members who addressed the house; and the rule is occasionally relaxed.
Accordingly I am inclined to think that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) should be permitted to proceed. In saying this, however, I should like to express the hope that all hon. members will bear in mind the necessity of discussing the principle of the bill, so that it may not be necessary for the Chair to qualify the indulgence which has been granted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time the discussion arose in regard to the point of order I was referring to the views which have been expressed by Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King in regard to the importance of publicity and its effect in dealing with this subject. Because of the fact that during the greater part of the time the present act has been in force he was Prime Minister of Canada, I should like to read into the record his remarks appearing at page 746 of Hansard for February 2, 1948, to indicate what he had to say as to the importance of the publication of reports. In doing so I recognize that this subject also has been discussed in a more limited way in the exchange of correspondence which was tabled here last Monday. This is what Mr. Mackenzie King had to say:
May I say that this desire to find the facts, making that the basic duty of the committee, is founded upon the very sound philosophy that in the cure of what one might call social wrongs or anti-social evils, those anti-social acts which adversely affect the great masses of the people in their individual lives and homes, publicity in regard to the facts is a much more effective remedy than penalty.
Whatever men may be in their individual lives, there is nothing they abhor more, if they have been guilty of any meanness or taken any undue advantage of their fellowmen, than to have that meanness exposed in public. In regard to this class of social wrong I believe that if there are people to-day in Canada who are hoarding where they should be selling, and if there are others who are profiteering where they should be glad to do what is fair, such people will quickly take notice of the fact that this House of Commons has appointed a committee which can go into any single phase of this problem and bring individuals from any part of the country to answer for situations in which they may be involved.
I for one firmly believe in the power of publicity when based on facts. Public opinion plays a very large part in determining the course of events and the conduct of human beings. However, if public opinion is to be effective and to be of national service, it is very important that opinion be fully and clearly informed. The trouble with the situation to-day is that there is not sufficient knowledge of the facts to enable public opinion to be formed intelligently.
I end the quotation there because I believe what was said on that occasion has a very direct bearing on the view that has been expressed here, that there should be more information in regard to certain facts. As far as the present bill is concerned, it makes certain limited proposals. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has given his reasons for the amendments he is proposing. He has suggested that those constitute only part of what had been discussed as a result of the recommendations of the combines investigation branch.
The reason for emphasizing what has taken place is this. In deciding what course should now be followed, it is essential that we
Combines Investigation Act recognize exactly what has been done already under the act as it stands. In order that there may be no suggestion that a review of this point will not be relevant to the subject matter in question, I indicated that I proposed to move an amendment that this whole matter be referred to an appropriate committee in order that further information might be obtained. If hon. members are to form an accurate judgment as to whether or not there is reason to place this question before a committee, it is essential that they examine what actually took place. Whether or not the report was correct in its conclusions, whether the commissioner may have overlooked some facts which should have been taken into consideration, or whether the report itself failed to show what the government regarded as adequate reasons for proceeding under the act, all have no bearing whatever upon the mandatory requirement that the report shall be published by the minister. In his letter of November 4 to Mr. McGregor the Minister of Justice gave this explanation for his failure to publish the report:
The government therefore took the responsibility of withholding publication of your report pending the amendment of the Combines Investigation Act to cure the difficulties created by the dental supplies judgment.
That reference can only be to the amendments now before us; therefore these very amendments bring directly into consideration the withholding of this report and the reasons for doing so. The government, through the Minister of Justice, was asked upon what authority it relied when it made its decision not to act under section 27, subsection 5, of the Combines Investigation Act. To this direct question the Minister of Justice is reported at page 1524 of Hansard as saying:
Well, Mr. Speaker, it relied upon the fact that any democratic government is answerable to the people of the country for its acts.
That statement, Mr. Speaker, is a challenge to our whole system of responsible government. It implies that the government has the right to make its decisions and then withhold any knowledge of those decisions as long as it sees fit. Then, at some future date, the government can let the public decide what they think about the limited information they have in regard to what took place. That is not our system. Our system is clear. The members are responsible to the people and the government is responsible to parliament. It is essential that we bear that in mind in reviewing what has taken place.
This report of the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act was delivered to the Department of Justice on December 29, 1948. The act required that the minister publish that report within fifteen days. It
1728	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act should have been published, therefore, by January 13. This house met on January 26. Assuming that the minister felt there might be good reasons for withholding publication, and that he thought he was justified in doing so, then at least it was his bounden duty to explain to the house as soon as it met that he had taken this course. This would have enabled parliament, to which the government is answerable, to express its opinion on that decision without delay. That was not done. There was no hint that this report was being suppressed. On the contrary the fact that the government continued to withhold any action, and that it did withhold this report until more than two years after the alleged offences had been committed, has perhaps resulted in the further fact that, no matter what case may be made by the report, no action can be taken. However, that is another subject.
Once again, might I emphasize that we are not called upon to pass upon the findings of the commissioner in determining the correctness or otherwise of the actions of the government in this case. What every member of this house should be concerned about is the unquestioned violation of the act by the Minister of Justice, and his unexplained failure to place this whole subject before the House of Commons after it met last January. If the facts were so clear, why was this whole question not placed before parliament at that time? Could there be the slightest doubt in the mind of any hon. member as to the real reason for suppressing this information? In explaining the violation of the act last Monday, the Minister of Justice said the government relied, as I have said before, upon the fact that it is answerable to the people. The government took extremely effective steps to see that the people had no knowledge of this matter when the people did have a chance to express their opinion.
These words of the Minister of Justice disclose a state of mind which makes this incident more serious than it already appeared to be. The government broke the law; there can be no dispute about that. Asked for an explanation, the Minister of Justice blandly replies, in effect, that the government is answerable, not to parliament but to the people at such time as they have a chance of expressing their opinion. This raises a far more serious issue than the violation of the Combines Investigation Act by the government, serious though that is. It is doubtful whether hon. members have been confronted with so serious a fundamental issue since confederation. The law which has been violated by the government was a law passed by parliament. It is all very well for the Minister of Justice to smile, but the very


fact that he smiles indicates how careless some members of the government have become about the constitutional practices upon which the survival of our system will ultimately depend.
One of the suggestions put forward in regard to this act and to the problems raised is that the act itself would be the basis upon which companies that had been doing a public service might be pilloried. In view of the fact that certain amendments are under discussion, necessarily the whole act is under consideration at the same time. It would be well to go back to the speech with which the present act was introduced in 1923. On May 7, 1923, the then Prime Minister emphasized something that seems to be overlooked by those who feel that the terms of the act may be unduly harsh. At page 2520 of Hansard of that date, Mr. Mackenzie King is reported as follows:
I notice that many of the newspapers of the country have reported that the government is endeavouring by this legislation to legislate against combines as such, to legislate against the right of manufacturers or merchants to fix a resale price. There is nothing of the kind in the legislation. As a matter of fact, it proceeds from a diametrically opposite point of view. I explained that, I think, pretty fully at the time of introducing the bill. It proceeds broadly on the theory that in this age of commercial and industrial competition, not merely between industry and industry and locality and locality, between the industries of one province and those of another, but between the industries of one country and those of another, the industries, one might almost say, of one continent and those of another, large combinations of capital, organizations of business in a large way, are an absolute essential if the business of our country is to hold its own in competition with the business of other countries. But just because it is recognized that it is necessary to have these large organizations of business, so the government recognizes that some restraint must be placed on the possible abuse of great power which may come into their hands.
It was for the purpose of restraining such possible abuses that this act was introduced. The act does not make every combine a law breaker, but the act prohibits only such combinations as are likely to operate to the detriment or against the interests of the public. Section 498 of the Criminal Code, which has been referred to by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), deals with the same subject, and also contains a similar limitation upon its effect because it provides that there is an offence only if there is an undue limitation of competition. What is undue or what is contrary to the public interest is for the courts to determine.
This matter is one which has been brought before the house by the exchange of correspondence. One of the things which hon. members should bear in mind is what was said by Mr. McGregor in his memorandum

accompanying his letter to the Minister of Justice. I quote from the second page of his memorandum:
There is greater need now for strong action under the combines act than there has been at any time in the past twenty-five years. To an alarming degree price fixing activities such as we reported in the flour milling industry have been developing in the post-war years; some of them originated in the war period; and some were started, as in the flour milling industry, even in the pre-war years. To meet the situation, to prevent these practices which are designed to limit or eliminate the public safeguard of price competition, there is every reason why the powers of the combines act should be strengthened. Council accepted in the present bill our proposals of three amendments, including a very important amendment designed to meet the difficulties of the dental judgment; but the only suggestions from the council which you called on me to consider seriously were provisions which would have had the result of limiting the effectiveness of the legislation.
I have in mind such proposals as those to eliminate the commissioner's initiative in launching inquiries, to place serious limitations on the requirement that reports be made public, and to provide for exemption, after prior approval, of certain types of agreements to restrict production or eliminate price competition. These suggestions have not been included in the present bill, but my understanding from you is that consideration of them has been merely postponed pending a proposed "overhauling" of the act. Overhauling of the act could serve many useful purposes. I am apprehensive, however, particularly in view of the nature of the changes which have been suggested for consideration, of the ultimate result of any revision of the statute which would include changes along these or similar lines.
Since this is a statement of the commissioner under the combines act it is of the utmost importance that hon. members know whether it does correctly interpret the situation which exists, because an understanding of that is essential if a sound decision is to be made in regard to the issue which is now before the house.
One thing, of course, that is always in the minds of hon. members when a matter of this kind is under discussion is what the position of the government is in regard to the numbers of hon. members who support it. The challenge that is now before the house is not merely as great a challenge to members of the opposition as it is a challenge to every member of the party who supports the government to reassert the responsibility of parliament on this occasion. After all, if the members of any party are simply to vote in accordance with the place where their names are included in the list of members of this house then it will be quite unnecessary to attend. The government could introduce its legislation and the vote could be taken on the basis of the numbers of members here, and the result would be in accordance with practice of that kind.
Our whole system has been based upon the assertion of members of every party of the basic principles of our parliamentary
Combines Investigation Act system. Certainly the government has a great majority, but let us remember that there has hardly been a time in the history of parliaments when the government was not reasonably assured of a majority in the house when it presented legislation. That is not the basis upon which debate proceeds. Debate proceeds on the assumption that hon. members will give it their consideration and vote in accordance with the reasons that are put forward and with the needs of the people of this country and the best interests of Canada as a whole. If our parliamentary system is in jeopardy, then those who have the greatest responsibility are those who constitute the majority. The greater the power the greater the responsibility, and in this case that responsibility is very heavy indeed.
I	propose to move an amendment,
Mr. Speaker, which will make it possible for hon. members to deal with it with the kind of information which they should have. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That the said bill be not now read the second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that they have power to send for persons, papers and records and that in addition to other recommendations with respect to the subject matter of the said bill they shall also have power to report upon the extent to which the effective administration of legislation relating to restrictive trade practices has been, or is being, prejudiced by the action of the government in failing to carry out the mandatory requirements of the existing law.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
This is an important debate from a number of points of view, not the least being the situation under which this matter was brought into the House of Commons. May I just summarize. Less than two weeks ago I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) a question as to whether a report had been made on the flour milling industry. He said that he would answer the question the next day. My colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), asked whether the commissioner under the act had resigned. The same answer was given. The next day we learned that a report had been made and that the commissioner had resigned. It was then we were told that this particular bill would be introduced to amend the Combines Investigation Act. It is safe to say that at least the introduction of this amending bill was expedited by the questions that were asked in the house, and that brought to light both the resignation of the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act and the fact that the report had been suppressed.
I want to say to the government and to hon. members that when the government

Combines Investigation Act took upon itself-and let us remember that the minister acted after having received advice from the government regarding this matter-to suppress the report it violated one of the fundamental principles of our parliamentary democracy. I have no recollection of anything of the kind being done in the course of our parliamentary history in Canada; but I would remind hon. members that in 1649 an English king was beheaded because he did exactly what the government has done in this connection. I would remind hon. gentlemen that in 1688-89 another king, James II, was compelled to vacate the British throne for doing precisely what the government has done in this connection.
While there are several of them, there are at least two basic documents upon which not only our own parliamentary democracy but the democracies of the United States and of all other English-speaking democracies are based-Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights.
The Bill of Rights was introduced into the British House of Commons in 1689. After reciting their grievances this is what it sets out in the very first two clauses:
And thereupon the said Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, pursuant to their respective letters and elections, being now assembled in a full and free representation of this nation, taking into their most serious consideration the best means for attaining the ends aforesaid, do in the first place (as their ancestors in like case have usually done) for the vindicating and asserting their ancient right and liberties, declare:
1.	That the pretended power of suspending of laws, or the execution of laws, by regal authority, without consent of parliament is illegal.
2.	That the pretended power of dispensing with laws, or the execution of laws, by regal authority, as it hath been assumed and exercised of late, is illegal.
I say to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that that is precisely what happened in connection with this report, namely that the government exercised a pretended power of dispensing with the execution of a law, a statute, passed by this parliament. And, having assumed that power, it exercised the power illegally.	.
Then, in our own parliamentary history, in 1873 in the House of Commons the Hon. Edward Blake, who I believe in those days was a member of the Liberal party, said this:
It makes no difference to a free people whether their rights are invaded by the crown-[DOT]
That is, by regal authority-
-or by the cabinet; what is material is to secure that they shall not be invaded at all.
I say in this connection that while we will support the amendment offered by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew) I regret that it is in the terms in which it is. I think what we should be doing in this house in the discussion this afternoon is moving a vote of

censure of the government, and asserting our right as a parliament to discipline the government for the breaking of the law of this land.
However, we will support the amendment [DOT] offered by the leader of the official opposition. As I have said, this matter is much more grave than appears on the surface, if we allow what has happened to go without complaint. If we allow the cabinet to usurp the rights of this parliament, to set aside acts of parliament and to neglect to fulfil and to execute the statutes of this parliament, we are jeopardizing the whole parliamentary system as we have known it throughout the years.
Let me say at the very outset that to my mind this is the fundamental issue in the debate. It is true that we are discussing amendments to an act on our statute books. But what use is it to discuss amendments to any act of parliament if the government arrogates to itself the right to set aside acts of parliament? What guarantee have we that these amendments now before the house will not be treated lightly by the government of this country? And I say to the Liberal majority in the house that if they are true to the principles of Liberalism they should be repeating what we have been saying in the house today, and what we said on that former occasion a short time ago when the matter was before the house.
And so, while we welcome these amendments, we feel the house should have had an opportunity of expressing itself with regard to the suppression of the report, to which reference has been made this afternoon. And I say this, that whether it was deliberate or not, the manner in which the previous debate was instituted the other afternoon precluded the possibility of the opposition-or indeed any member in the house-calling upon the house to make an effective protest by way of a vote. That prevented a discussion-and I am glad, Mr. Speaker, that your ruling today was such that it does not rule out entirely references to the grave matters to which I have just referred.
This also I wish to say, that the party I have the privilege of leading in the house has always been keenly interested in this particular type of legislation. From time to time we have raised the question of the growing trustification of this country, of the participation of powerful interests in Canada in international cartels. Sometimes we have felt that very little attention was being paid by some hon. members to these matters, and that very little care was being exercised in connection with them.
I say I am glad this legislation has been introduced, because two years ago within a couple of weeks, after a conversation with the

present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who was then secretary of state for external affairs, I wrote him a letter which I wish now to bring to the attention of the house to indicate how interested we have been over the years in these matters. I shall quote the material part of this letter dated at Ottawa December 4, 1947, as follows:
As far as I have been able to find out, there appear to be both price agreements and monopolies, which I readily admit are rather difficult to detect, but which, from all appearances, certainly exist and should be investigated.
My fear is that our legislation regarding the control of monopolies, is inadequate, and the needs of the present situation far beyond the scope of our present staff, which is much too small.
However, my opinion is that monopolies, in various degrees, exist in aluminum, cement, our principal chemicals, in rayon yarn, in the production of steel rails, and, of course, in nickel, lead, some iron and steel products, and some nonferrous metal products.
As to price agreements, I think it is pretty well known that, where there is any competition in fertilizers, price agreements exist. It was well established-although an appeal, owing to the death of the judge, was not made-that the tobacco products are subject to price agreements and price fixing; also it was established that rubber footwear and the principal leather industries have agreements regarding prices, and that there are large areas of plumbing and heating equipment and hardware products in which there are price agreements.
You will recollect too, that the moving picture industry was acquitted on technical grounds of combination in 1931.
Price spreads investigation made some disclosures regarding the manner in which live stock prices appeared to be agreed upon each day, by Canada Packers and Swift Canadian. In the opinion of persons who have had personal experience with these two companies, and whom I know well, these practices continued after the investigation, and may still continue. In any event, these seem to be operations into which investigation is warranted.
Early in the 1920's, the fruit wholesale monopoly was investigated by, I believe, the Duncan commission, and certain disturbing facts were established. As lately as 1939, a combine was reported by the commissioner, in the wholesaling of fruits and vegetables in western Canada. Again, the action failed on-what appeared to be-highly technical grounds, and there was no appeal.
In view, however, of the recent increases in prices, I should think that immediate fields for an investigation might be fertilizers, canned goods, textiles, rubber footwear, and, I would include, farm implements-about which a parliamentary committee made a report in 1937.
I realize that this is a pretty formidable list, but I do not think that, even then, it is exhaustive. In my opinion, Canadian industry has become more and more under the domination of monopolies, and more and more guilty of price fixing; in other words, I believe that competition in many major lines of endeavour is non-existent.
I thought I would read that letter lest it be said that we are taking advantage of the introduction of this legislation to talk about combines without having suggested anything in regard to meeting this situation from time to time. As I said in that letter two years ago, the legislation we have had
Combines Investigation Act on the statute books has been inadequate and we welcome the amendments that have been introduced. However, in voting, as I expect we shall do, to refer the subject matter to a committee of this house, we are not in any way trying to delay the passage of this measure. Arising out of the meetings of that committee might conceivably come recommendations for the further strengthening of the Combines Investigation Act. However, much as I welcome these amendments, I do not think they are exhaustive by any means.
As I have said for years, Canadian industries have been subject to the control of powerful nation-wide monopolies and combinations. The competitive system upon which the free enterprise system, as my hon. friends like to call the present system, relies has been quite largely destroyed in our country. If we accept the definition that competition involves primarily competition in price among manufacturers and producers, then I submit that there is no competition at all in major sectors of our national economy.
I learned from the classical economists, which I used to study years ago and which I occasionally read from time to time, that the very basis of regulation in an unplanned or free enterprise system, such as was defended and indeed visualized in the early years of this and the last century by the economists of the capitalist era, is that each manufacturer or producer decides independently of all other manufacturers or producers of the same class what the selling price of his article shall be. That was a classical definition.
The fact that we have manufacturers producing the same type of article competing and advertising for sales does not involve real competition in price which, as I have said, must be present if we accept the classical position as the basis for competition in a free enterprise or capitalist system. The feature of the Canadian economy today which has been developed since the early days of the present century is that few producers or manufacturers of basic commodities have survived. The number has been whittled down until it can be said that just a handful of manufacturers dealing with a particular commodity-this is illustrated in the report of the flour milling industry that has been placed before the house-have succeeded in occupying a monopoly position where they get together and decide that there will be no competition in prices.
This is particularly true in certain of our great industries. For example, in oil we have Imperial Oil. In the chemical industry we have Canadian Industries Limited. The same applies to the iron and steel industry. In the case of farm implements it was shown

Combines Investigation Act conclusively before the parliamentary committee which sat in 1936 and 1937, as it was shown before the Saskatchewan legislative committee and before a committee of the congress of the United States, that the farm implement business was dominated by two great companies, International Harvester and John Deere. We all Should know the story of cement in this country where Canada Cement has a complete monopoly. The brewing and hard liquor industries are in the same position. The hard liquor industry is monopolized by one, two or three firms. While there may be more than two or three firms in the brewing industry, price levels are maintained.
The reports by the investigators under the Combines Investigation Act have shown conclusively that price agreements eliminating price competition have been arrived at. We have reports before us dealing with dental supplies, bread baking, optical goods, tobacco, fruits and so on, while parliamentary and legislative committees, as I have pointed out, have shown that the same sort of thing is to be found in the field of farm implements. The situation revealed in western Canada in connection with the bread baking industry is such that prosecutions should be proceeded with by the federal authorities.
As has already been indicated, we 'have the report on the flour milling industry which the government concealed and now states its refusal to act upon.
In addition to the amendments being introduced at this time, I think amendments should be introduced to the Criminal Code whereby combinations of this sort extending over long periods of years can be prosecuted, not only for what may have been done in the last two years but for what may have been done throughout their entire history as a combination. The alleged limitation in the Criminal Code in connection with this particular type of combination and price fixing should be removed and any companies involved should be held accountable for anything done over a reasonable period of years.
The facts are self-evident and there is no question in my mind that under the act as it now stands the flour milling industry could have been attacked successfully earlier this year had the report of its operations been made public and had the government proceeded to take action against them.
I say that the flour milling interests could have been attacked successfully for their operations during the war period. Not one tittle of evidence has been produced to show that the government, the wartime prices and trade board, or any of its officers, authorized the stifling of competition between December, 1941, and September 15, 1947, when I understand these investigations were started, and
[Mr. Coldwell.l

commenced incidentally, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said today and as I said the other day, with the knowledge and the approval of the then minister of justice, the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley. From having studied the report I say that I believe, under the unamended terms of the act, there was an excellent chance of succeeding with the prosecution of the flour milling industry for its activities during the war period.
As the minister knows, I have asked for documentary evidence to support the contention that what the flour milling industry did in the war years was done with the authority of the wartime prices and trade board. I have been told that considerable research is necessary in order to produce any such documents. Consequently I think it is pretty safe to assume that up to the present time neither Mr. Gordon, nor any of his wartime officers, nor the minister, are aware of any documentary evidence or any authority given directly or indirectly, under which the milling industry maintained high prices and endeavoured to eliminate price competition in their industry in the war years.
For a moment I want to refer to one or two parts of the report to substantiate what I say. For, while the amendment is designed to strengthen the act, and we welcome it, have we any assurance that when we pass the legislation and the act is strengthened this matter will be proceeded with and these great interests prosecuted? On June 12, 1942, we find this:
. . . now that the export business has been so drastically reduced, higher prices in the domestic market are inevitable. Unless export business picks up, it will certainly be necessary for the mills to come to some agreement to maintain ceiling prices and we believe efforts will be made along this line shortly.
Let me point out that ceiling prices were authorized but minimum prices were never authorized. The other day-I thought rather unfairly-the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), or was it Mr. Gordon in the document which the minister read, compared the milling interests with the gasoline interests. I believe it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That is an entirely different situation. The wartime prices and trade board set a fixed price on gasoline. It could not go up; it could not go down. They set a ceiling not a floor on cereal products, including flour. One gentleman, Mr. Soward, wrote to the officers of his company, the Maple Leaf Milling Company, and on October 5, 1942, an informal meeting of the executive committee was held and the following recommendations were made for submission at the next executive meeting:
It was realized that the first step to be taken in respect of correcting certain conditions within, the

industry, in so far as our members are concerned, was to petition the flour administrator to establish uniform ceilings on flour for the different categories of trade, based on the highest ceilings which any mill could establish, and which would constitute a uniform price. The next step considered necessary was a guarantee by all mills to advance to, and maintain their prices at, the ceilings established.
In this respect, however, the view was expressed that perhaps all mills could not sell at the same price in all sections of eastern Canada, and as a means of overcoming that difficulty it was suggested that any mill would have the privilege of declaring, in meeting, its intention to sell (in territories designated by the mill) at a discretionary price of 10 cents per barrel under the uniform prices set by the flour administrator.
While such a submission was subsequently made to the flour administrator, uniform prices were never established by the wartime prices and trade board. Indeed, the establishment of a uniform structure and prices was finally agreed upon by the industry for the province of Quebec, and at a meeting of the Quebec sales managers on November 2 a proposed new selling structure and prices were set up. I bring that to the attention of the house because that was wartime, 1942. Wherever we look in the report we find that, while the wartime prices and trade board set ceilings, they did not set floors. Whatever the association may have tried to do, reading the report I can find no evidence to support the suggestion that they did so by authority of the wartime prices and trade board. I could go on reading extract after extract from their minutes to bear out what I say. For example, there are the minutes of the meeting of the association of the 21st of April, 1942, reading:
Arising out of a long discussion of recent developments in certain centres (Kamloops, Calgary and Trail were cited as cases in point), the following resolution was unanimously adopted.
"There shall be no reduction in the dealer structure by any kind of independent action to meet any local price situation. Each situation as it arises shall be reported to the secretary as the means to obtain complete executive action."
Then I find this in the minutes of October 21, 1943:
The dealer list is to be maintained without deviation in all classes and categories of the trade.
It is the association's decision, not that of the wartime prices and trade board. Who was the controller? The controller was the manager of one of the great milling companies. Again I emphasize that, in my opinion, without strengthening the act-and I am glad it is being strengthened-a prosecution could have been undertaken under the old act with at least some chance of success. Again I want to emphasize that the wartime prices and trade board set maximum prices, and as far as I can find anywhere in the report they gave no authority which would justify the actions of the association. I look forward to
Combines Investigation Act seeing what the minister can produce in the course of the next day or two. So far as I can see the board gave no authority to sellers to combine to prevent price reductions below the ceiling level; indeed, quite the opposite.
On May 26, 1947, just before controls were removed, we find documentary evidence to show conclusively that the association was endeavouring to force some companies to maintain prices which those companies did not think they needed to maintain. It is the same with mill feed, a very important item to our farmers. In the minutes of an executive meeting of August 18, 1944, I find the following:
Members of the Alberta group shall take immediate steps to examine the basis of sales of coarse grains and mill feed, interior British Columbia, and so be prepared to resolve the common problem at the next executive meeting.
Therefore I say that this matter is of paramount importance from two points of view. The first point of view which I mentioned was the importance to the life of this parliament, the preservation of our democratic institutions in Canada, of our adherence to parliamentary practice, and indeed more than that, of our adherence to the basic principles of the Bill of Rights and the rule of law. I say, further, that as far as the evidence goes, in the report we have read during the last few days no suggestion can be found anywhere that at any time Mr. Donald Gordon or Mr. Ken Taylor gave any assurance to the milling industry or encouraged them to maintain prices at the maximum ceiling level. No action was taken by the wartime prices and trade board to set a floor price, nor was any encouragement given the milling industry to prevent reductions in domestic prices.
Now let us take a look at a paragraph on page 115 of the report which I am going to read because it has a bearing on the discussion we have heard in this house:
Simultaneous and uniform price increases were put into effect on September 15, 1947, when the wheat subsidy was withdrawn and flour prices were decontrolled. Flour was increased by $4.05 per barrel and mill feeds by $10 per ton. While the investigation which followed disclosed little documentary proof of agreement on these particular price increases . . .
Indeed, if I may say so, the people who were investigated denied that there was any agreement.
. . . examination of company and association records disclosed a series of price fixing agreements over a period of years. In the oral hearings association members contended that the uniform price increases in September had not been determined by agreement. . . .
Yet last week we were told that on September 15, when the controls were coming off, Mr. Ken Taylor got in touch with the flour controller and together they agreed on an. increase of $4.05 per barrel.

Well, I am going to continue reading the paragraph I was quoting when interrupted:
In the oral hearings association members contended that the uniform price increases in September had not been determined by agreement, although some members admitted that prior to decontrol they had discussed their increased costs. The only discussion of the subject recorded in the confidential memoranda in the east was at a meeting on March 21, 1947, when agreement was reached to convene the eastern sales managers "for the purpose of arriving at proper selling structures in preparation for decontrol: the combined views to be considered by the general sales managers in meeting."
My hon. friend has just drawn to my attention that in his speech on November 7 the Minister of Justice said:
After considerable remonstrance and discussion the millers accepted $4.05 for flour and a price of $10 for mill feed, the desire being that the price of flour should, not be held down at the cost of having mill feed rise too high.
I thought the other figures were given at that time also.

speechtext:
That would be contrary to the act. That is price fixing. As a matter of fact price control was a matter of ceilings, not floors, and there was no reason in the world why the flour millers should all raise their prices by $4.05 a barrel. That is the point.
So, Mr. Speaker, one could go on quoting from this report to show that throughout the wartime period the milling interests got together, disciplined one another if there were any inclination to sell below the ceiling price, and did everything they could to maintain a price that was high. In fact in one place they say they wanted the ceiling fixed at the very highest level that could be attained by any one of them. So I think the

evidence before us is of such a nature as to bring them within the meaning of combination and price fixing under the act we are proposing to amend today. Let me quote further from page 114 of Mr. McGregor's report:
The practice during the war years to which exception is taken in this report is the same practice to which exception is taken with respect to other times, that of agreements to remove competition in price. In the war years regulations established maximum levels beyond which prices could not be increased. In this period concerted efforts were made to prevent competition by securing agreement as to the prices which the members would follow. Such joint action was neither required nor sanctioned by the prices board or any other government agency. Board policy was definitely directed to the maintenance of competitive conditions with respect to prices.
That is what the public of Canada understood throughout the entire period of the war. It is all very well for the milling interests to say that they were authorized to do these things when no authority can be found. Indeed, in Mr. Gordon's own statement, which was read into the record at page 1502 of Hansard of this year, Mr. Donald Gordon said -I am omitting some words which do not alter the meaning:
-the ceiling price-would naturally become the fixed price and, such being the case, any "agreement" in respect of prices would have been meaningless.
If you look across at the next column on the same page, about the middle of the column, you will find Mr. Gordon says this: -no practical system of uniform prices was ever discovered and it remained in the realm of wishful thinking throughout the period of control.
In order to be fair, perhaps I should read the next sentence:
Nevertheless, I have no doubt that the flour administrator in collaboration with the industry did his utmost to insure orderly conditions in the industry in the interests of maintaining supply as well as price stability.

On page 36 of the report we find the following:
On September 15, Lake of the Woods, Maple Leaf, McDonald and Robb, Ogilvie, Purity, Quaker, Robin Hood and St. Lawrence all increased the price of hard wheat flour by $4.05 per barrel and mill feeds by $10 per ton.
Now, what about this? The report says:
In the course of the oral examination of representatives of the member companies of C.N.M.A., it was contended that the amount of the advances had not been reached by agreement, although it was admitted by some that prior to decontrol they had discussed with others the increased costs with which they were faced. It was also contended that the amount of the flour increase was not in fact sufficient to cover all increases in costs which had arisen since the basic period in 1941.
Again and again in this report the milling representatives deny that there were agreements. Yet, running all through this report- I am speaking of the war years now because the other evening I dealt with the years prior to the war-in the correspondence, the memoranda and the minutes there are indications that every attempt was made to secure price agreements.
On May 16, 1943, a discussion ensued with respect to the recent notification to mills that the price of flour in respect of ships' stores business, or at least in respect of quotations to the Department of Munitions and Supply had been decontrolled. The report says:
Finally it was agreed that in connection with the Department of Munitions and Supply, quotations in so far as Halifax is concerned, shall be made in behalf of all members by Mr. A. G.

There is to be no competition. The millers decided, in spite of the fact that the Department of Munitions and Supply was to buy decontrolled supplies, there would be no competition.
On May 18, 1943, the agreement was explained by D. A. Campbell, the St. Lawrence Company, to A. G. Watson, sales manager at Halifax, as follows:
At a meeting of the executive of the Millers' Association today, the perennial question of prices for ship's stores came up for discussion, and it was the unanimous opinion that you should take over the selling of ship's stores for all of the mills (in Halifax), and that Whitney would perform the same service in Saint John. By "ship's stores" was meant the quotations to the Department of Munitions and Supply, and did not refer to the supplies for oceangoing vessels, for which there does not seem to be a great deal of difficulty.
When the Department of Munitions and Supply called for tenders, expecting some competition in prices, the millers took steps to see that there was no competition in prices. They had one person setting the prices. In the debate a week ago I drew attention to the fact that in Vancouver they had a formula whereby the various prices were changed around to meet the demand for competitive prices, which defeated that objective altogether.

To us the Combines Investigation Act should be so strengthened as to ensure two important things for the Canadian people. The first is the establishment in our country of a condition of free enterprise, of free competition. I want to emphasize a condition of free competition. There cannot be freedom in any sense of the word for the average run of Canadian people if we have not freedom of competition in Canadian business.
We do not want to see large accumulations of capital wielding such power as to be a danger to the Canadian people. We do not want to see small companies destroyed, driven out of business through larger companies and combines exercising undue influence either with governments or under law. We have been fighting as strongly as it has been possible for us to fight for a condition of competition, because we feel that therein lie the seeds of success of the private enterprise system. Deny the right of real competition and you deny private enterprise, and you play into the hands of those people who constantly say, "There is an example of private enterprise for you",-the people who declare that one of the reasons why this act is being amended today is that we are admitting that private enterprise has failed.
I deny that. Private enterprise has not failed. We have to admit honestly that there are abuses of private enterprise, and it is those abuses we are trying now to obviate, to make impossible. I say now that that is the true function of government, to lay down such conditions as will regulate and make possible a system of private enterprise in the interests of all the people.
The second thing we believe a strong and effective Combines Investigation Act should do is protect the people of the country from the power that is often wielded by the accumulation of capital, for the purpose of establishing monopoly control in their interests. We have no truck or traffic with such breaches of decency. We condemn it in the strongest possible way; and when I say that we condemn it, we condemn the irresponsible use of power in the hands of people who have accumulated vast wealth and use it for their own selfish ends.
But happily that has not been the rule in this country. Though we have frequent examples of combines, and attempts at combines, I am happy to stand here and say that from my observation it has been the exception and not the rule. But the combines act ought to provide protection for the people

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part briefly in the debate this afternoon. In doing so might I point out that as head of a municipality for many years, particularly after the first great war, I noticed marked increases and spreads in prices. I saw the effect of those conditions upon the working classes in my city, and upon the small farmers.
I rise to support the amendment of my leader, which states-
That the said bill be not now read the second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that they have power to send for persons, papers and records and that in addition to other recommendations with respect to the subject matter of the said bill they shall also have power to report upon the extent to which the effective administration of legislation relating to restrictive trade practices has been, or is being, prejudiced by the action of the government in failing to carry out the mandatory requirements of the existing law.
That is a good motion, and a lifesaving motion for the government, as well. Speaking as a private member, may I say that the government often forgets that the private member is the connecting link between the government of the day and the electors. Where he ceases to function and permits himself to become a yes-man or a nodder, parliamentary government is at an end.

The people back in the constituencies do not expect hon. members in any part of the house to act as yes-men or nodders in days like these. Those who have sent us here are the ones who suffer from sky-high prices.
I remember in 1917 when there was a serious coal famine in our city, but at that time the price of Pennsylvania hard coal was only about $6 per ton. Today the price has skyrocketed until it is up to $23.50, and when you allow $1.50 to the retail man for delivering, it totals $25 per ton. It is fortunate that owing to Providence we have had a mild fall so that little coal has been used.
As far as I can see, the government has dealt with this report as a matter of policy rather than as a matter of law. The government apparently does not acknowledge what it owes to the opposition for the support they are being given in this amendment. This amendment will act as a lifesaver. I remember back in the thirties when we had the Stevens committee and it is most regrettable that we lost the services of Mr. Stevens, who had the support of the white-collar workers in Ontario. The work of that committee in connection with price spreads was one of the most important tasks ever done by a committee of this house.
Governments begin to die the moment they are born. I am not a bigoted party man. I submit that as a House of Commons we should seek to carry one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ. I referred to St. Luke the 11th chapter the other day and to what He had said about lawyers. A few years ago we had a select committee of the house, the Stevens committee, which went into the whole question of prices and spreads. It will be noticed that the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) would give the committee power to send for persons, papers and records. The committee would be entitled to send for crown officers and examine them as to why the law was not carried out. They could deal with the decision of Mr. Justice Barlow who ruled that there had been no proof that the directors of the companies charged had a guilty mind, which must be proved in the case of corporations.
I followed the work of Mr. McGregor in connection with the electrical combines case and other matters like that where it was found that they were interlocked and there was no way of attacking them. As I 'said the other day in connection with this matter, combines have flourished in Canada like the green bay tree. That is something which cannot be contradicted. We had an example the other day in connection with coal, and we have
Combines Investigation Act another example in connection with telephones where one company has jurisdiction over the two central provinces and is interlocked with Northern Electric. They are now proposing to increase the rates which will mean that a telephone is just a luxury. That is just one other industry that I can mention.
This committee will have the power to send for the law officers of the crown and find out why this is going on. The Stevens committee on prices and spreads found out in 1934. They represented the white-collar workers all over Ontario, the small mill man and so on.
In the days of Sir John Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier nearly everyone in Canada owned some property in the form of a small farm, a small mill, a blacksmith shop, a grocery store, a team and wagon, a country general store and things like that. In those days Canada was a nation of property owners. In the city from which I come sixty-five per cent of the people owned their own homes. Land was cheap and they could buy for as low as $6 per foot, the civic car lines gave them service, and they were able to build houses all over the city. Now that has all passed away and we are no longer a city of home owners because many have lost their homes because of high taxes and the high cost of living.
This committee should be established and it should follow the practices followed by the Stevens committee. It should go over this report and send for the crown officers. Last spring I contended that these trusts and combines in restraint of trade were flourishing like the green bay tree. At that time I gave a list of them extending from the Ottawa river to the Nipigon, the companies that controlled coal, copper, tin, zinc, platinum, asbestos, aluminum and many other commodities. All these companies are controlled from New York. I believe in the policy of Canada for Canadians.
I referred to the work of Lord Hewart on the new despotism in which he complained about the rules and regulations which permitted the restraint of trade and all that kind of thing. I hope when this committee meets it will tackle this problem in the right way. If they do they will find that what I say is correct. No doubt the report on the milling industry will be before the committee and they can send for Mr. McGregor or any others who have anything to do with it. The government policy has been all wrong. As I say, they have dealt with this whole problem as a question of policy, rather than as a question of law. The government had the power to act, but they did not go ahead. The report speaks for itself and I am not going to repeat what was said the other day by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).

Combines Investigation Act
We have now reached a position where the cabinet have ruled the roost long enough, and it is the duty of private members to regain some control over administration. The actions of the cabinet put me in mind of the days of the Family Compact when the executive tried to usurp the powers of the crown. You know what happened then. The actions of the government resemble those in a star chamber proceeding. We are back in the days when governments assumed liabilities and responsibilities beyond their powers, and usurped the functions of the House of Commons. If the executive want to rule the roost that way, then we might as well all go home. The duties of members of the House of Commons and of the Senate have been automatically abolished by such procedure. When did that happen? Fifteen days after the 29th of December, 1948, when the report should have been tabled. It should have been made available then to every member of the house, instead of being withheld until after the election. It was just pigeonholed. It was the duty of the proper minister of the crown to lay it on the table of the house, thus making it available to the house and to the country.
After all, who is paying for the report? No member of the cabinet is paying for it. It is paid for by the working classes, the large and small taxpayers. By way of income tax, sales tax and other taxes, the city of Toronto contributes almost one-third of the cash taxes of the whole dominion. It is not the cabinet's money; it belongs to the people who pay taxes. In the city of Toronto, a constituency of which I represent, they are paying almost one-third of it. It is an industrial city, and yet it has no member of the cabinet at the present time. That is one feature of the new despotism which is referred to in Lord Hewart's work, namely, where cabinets usurp the functions of parliament.
I believe the day has come when no minister of the crown should act in such a way. I appeal to the younger private members on the government benches. After all is said and done, the motion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) will act as a lifesaver for them when they go back to their constituencies because it will afford a proper investigation of the whole question of monopolies and restraint of trade. So far as municipalities are concerned, it has been a dead letter for a long time. Nothing was done about the coal famine in Toronto and many other monopolies which we have had. The records would also be before the house.
I do not wish to refer particularly to Mr. McGregor's report because it may not be quite in order to do so. His conclusions are as clear as crystal. The leader of the opposition


referred to them. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low) also referred to them and read certain extracts from the report. The report shows that the large milling companies sought to drive the smaller companies out of business. It shows that the larger companies were interlocked. There is no doubt about it, if you have a committee the officials can be summoned before it.
I wish we had had this report at the time of the Stevens inquiry. That preceded this report, and I should like to quote what some of the members said about the Stevens report and the good work that was done. You will have an opportunity to go into these matters at the proper time if the measure is referred to a committee. In the section of the report dealing with Mr. McGregor's conclusions I find the following:
This report follows another report on a related subject, an alleged combine in the bread baking industry in western Canada. Both reports disclose developments of much the same character-control of the industry concentrated in a few very large corporations and the efforts made under the leadership of the dominant groups to control competitive activity. They describe measures which have been taken to link the two industries by means of the financial control of some chain bakery companies by some flour milling companies and how this limiting of competitive purchases by the baking industry has had its impact on the flour milling industry. Each group within its own field has sought in its own way to attain the objective of eliminating price competition as a factor in business enterprise. This report is concerned with the measures taken by the principal flour milling companies which have been associated in the Canadian National Millers Association and C.N.M.A. (western division).
And also to some extent in the eastern division. There is no doubt that there was collusion. The report shows it, and the evidence shows it. Mr. McGregor winds up his report-and this is all I shall have to say about the report-by directing the attention of the minister to certain facts. I find these words in Mr. McGregor's conclusions:
The disruption of the restrictive agreements which infrequently did occur as a result of such market conditions cannot be regarded as a substitute for the safeguard of freedom of competition which should prevail as a general characteristic of business enterprise.
In another place I find these words:
The potential and actual operations of small mills and the presence of surplus capacity in the large mills, it was argued, would operate to prevent any effective agreement by the larger mills to curtail their competition in price in any substantial degree. The argument advanced was that each company with surplus capacity would actively compete with the others to get that volume of business which would enable it to keep its mills operating at the highest capacity possible.
That did not work out as shown by the definition of a combine in the Combines Investigation Act. The report goes on:
The definition of a "combine" in the Combines Investigation Act includes a combination carried on

by agreements having or designed to have certain effects, such as the fixing of common prices and the lessening of competition, which has operated or is likely to operate to the detriment or against the interest of the public.
The report goes on to quote from the decision of Mr. Justice Raney in Rex. v. Alexander, 1932, 2 Dominion Law Reports, page 123. The commissioner decided that the language used by Mr. Justice Raney would be applicable to this case. The quotation given in the report reads:
But the system adopted by the Electrical Estimators Association is not to be judged by its accidents, but by its tendency-not by the circumstance that sometimes the members of the association made no profit, or sometimes made too much, but by what the thing was in essence that the defendants were seeking to accomplish. That thing was the prevention or lessening of competition.
There is no doubt that the western and eastern divisions of the milling association tried to control their prices. You will notice that the prices in the eastern and western divisions were all top prices. They were up at the ceiling all the time, not the floor. All the business they did with the government was at ceiling prices. There was no floor price at all. The evidence shows that they interfered with the small millers, such as at Midland and others, and if a committee is set up that evidence will be before it in restraint of trade.
As far as I can see, in this case we have the cabinet on the one hand and the House of Commons on the other; and for all this house knows about these matters we might just as well all go home and let the executive rule the roost and run the show, assuming the functions of both houses of parliament. Within fourteen days after December 29 of last year the public were entitled to learn about the report made by this government official. It was not a secret report; it was an open report made under the act. The cabinet were not entitled to see that report first; far from it. The people who paid for the report were entitled to learn the gist of it, as they have been told about other reports. Every department of the government is doing this sort of thing, keeping information from the public who pay for it.
Publicity has been the greatest deterrent in preventing monopolies and restraint of trade in this country. Away back in 1934 the Stevens committee did more to call attention to monopolies and the way restraint of trade was flourishing in Canada than has been done since confederation. That committee electrified the public by the way it conducted its business, and did a great work for the people of this country. I am a party man, I suppose, because I am a Conservative. I may be the only one left, I do not know; but I have supported certain definite principles ever
Combines Investigation Act since I have been a member of the house. Sometimes I think it would be far better if we made this a national party, and not something like what they have in Manitoba and British Columbia. When our late leader, Lord Bennett, was with us we were a national party. He was a supporter of a wide open inquiry. It was not the case, as Saturday Night says, that nothing was done. More was done by the Stevens committee on price spreads and their regulation than by all the Saturday Nights I ever read, so they are not correct in that statement. That committee had the complete support of the government of that day.
So I wish to record my protest against the way this matter has been handled. I have never had any confidence in these monopolies in restraint of trade. They seem to go on forever; and they will continue in Canada until we have a House of Commons composed of members who will cease to be yes-men and in restraint of trade. They seem to go on nodders.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment. I would have preferred a motion that would amount to a vote of censure upon the government but I think perhaps the amendment is more realistic, for I cannot imagine anything this government might do that would induce its overwhelming number of supporters to endorse a vote of censure against it.
I am quite sure there is justification for sending the bill to a committee. For a moment I want to touch upon the withholding of the McGregor report, and the attitude of the minister and the cabinet toward that action. I doubt if there has been another instance of this kind in all Canadian history. Here we had a cabinet minister, with the approval of his associates, deliberately violating a statute passed by parliament, going through months when parliament was in session and hiding that information from parliament. Then we had the government going through a general election, still withholding that information from the electorate; we had them going through a miniature election, in a whole series of by-elections, still withholding that information, and not until those byelections were out of the way was it possible to drag this information from the cabinet. As I have said, I doubt whether there has been another instance of this kind in the history of the Canadian parliament.
I want to emphasize, as did the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and other speakers, the seriousness of that situation as it affects our parliamentary system. If we are going to accept the principle that a cabinet minister or a cabinet

Combines Investigation Act may with impunity disregard legislation passed by parliament; that a ministry can meet parliament without divulging such information; that a government can go to the country in a general election and withhold it, and go through a series of by-elections still without divulging it, where are we? What becomes of our parliamentary system? If the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the cabinet are above the law, what is the use of having laws enacted by this parliament? That is the situation which must be faced, and because it is so serious I regret it is not possible at this time to bring in a motion of censure on the government.
The minister has referred to his responsibility and that of the cabinet to the country. As has been pointed out already, he has entirely overlooked the fact that all through Canadian parliamentary history it has been an accepted principle that the cabinet is responsible to the House of Commons. Cabinet ministers are elected, as all other hon. members are elected, as representatives of constituencies. They are appointed to the cabinet by the Prime Minister. The cabinet is directly responsible to the elected representatives of the people. If we accept the suggestion of the minister that they are directly responsible to the country, what becomes of their responsibility to this house? Here they withhold information from the electorate, and rely upon the fact that the public has a short memory and probably will be induced to forget this incident within the next four years, before the government must go to the country again. To properly describe this action I would have to use language which would not be parliamentary, so I shall content myself with saying that this whole matter produces a very unpleasant odour.

That is what I mean. There are good reasons, Mr. Speaker, why a committee should be set up. There are some things this house should know. We have received from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) one reason for the withholding of this report. In the daily press we have read a report, published with the approval of the combines commissioner, which is completely at variance with the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this house. Both these statements cannot be right. One or the other is wrong. I submit that before the members can vote intelligently on the second reading of this bill, there should be an opportunity to bring Mr. McGregor before a committee of this house to get his side of the story. Then we could attempt to find out, if possible, which of these two statements is the correct one.

There are other things we should know. It has already been pointed out that this act has been in force for approximately twenty years. It is only now that the government has discovered that the act cannot be enforced. I believe the house should have the opportunity of ascertaining whether recommendations have been made to the government during those years for amendments to this act. The members should have the opportunity of ascertaining whether the commissioner, who was responsible for the enforcement of this act, or the government has been at fault for leaving the act on the statute books for twenty years and only now discovering that it cannot be enforced.
Furthermore, there has been a suggestion that the proposed amendments to the act will not do the job the act was designed to do. I submit this house should have an opportunity of finding out whether those amendments will provide the necessary machinery to secure convictions or whether there should be other amendments than those which are proposed. These are some of the questions which I believe should be discussed and to which some answers should be found. These answers can be found only in a committee.
I should like to go one step further. While we are overhauling this Combines Investigation Act, I think it is about time this parliament set up a select committee on small business. There is ample evidence in this report that the particular industry under investigation attempted, apparently with success, to squeeze the small concerns out of business. It is no secret that that is happening all across the country. Numerous reports have been submitted indicating that chain stores and large industries deliberately force small businesses out of existence. I would think that this government, which prides itself on maintaining the free enterprise system, would show some concern for the small businessman at this time in our history. I believe there are approximately
120,000	to 125,000 small businessmen in Ontario alone. I would think such a government would show some concern for the protection of these men.
I suggest that consideration be given to the establishment of a select committee of this house on small businesses. I know the minister's answer. I know the attitude other cabinet ministers have taken when members have suggested that other committees, such as the veterans committee, be set up. Their attitude has been that the cabinet is responsible for these things. I know there is a difference between our system of cabinet government and the United States system. Accepting the principle that the cabinet is responsible to parliament, then we suggest

there is a place for these committees to advise, to investigate, to acquire data and to enable the members of the house to serve a more useful purpose than merely being rubber stamps for a Liberal cabinet. If the cabinet is prepared to restore to this House of Commons a vestige of the authority that is historically its right instead of attempting to assume full control in its own hands, then these committees could be set up.
Therefore I would ask the minister, when he is overhauling this Combines Investigation Act, to give consideration to setting up a select committee of the house on small businesses, similar to that which is functioning in Washington. I have reports of the meetings, investigations and recommendations of that committee. In so far as there exist in the business world of this country situations that are similar to those in the United States, I would urge that my suggestion be taken into consideration.
