speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at recess I had just mentioned the fact that the effect of holding up the report until the month of November had the result of actually preventing any prosecution taking place.
It was some three years ago, when the amendments were before the house, that I suggested that certain changes be made. One of them, accepted by the then minister of justice, the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), had the effect of allowing any person in this country to take proceedings for alleged infractions of the Combines Investigation Act. Up to that time it was impossible for a private person so to do.

The result of holding up the report, therefore, has been that the right of every or any person in this country enjoyed under that amendment to take proceedings has in fact been entirely denied.
One other matter to which I should like to refer has to do with the question of publicity. There are some who feel that publicity in advance of a trial is a denial of the principles of British common law and our own traditions, and that while a report may be made to the minister, it ought not to be published. I raised that point myself in 1948 in connection with the optical case.
As an answer to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) I should like to read the reply of the then minister of justice, the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, as it appears at page 4919 of Hansard for June 8, 1948, where he stated:
As I said the other day when the hon. member raised this question on the orders of the day, that section or a similar section has been in the act from 1910 down to the present time. Of course, from 1923 until 1935, I think, the registrar was the important man; the general course was that the registrar made an investigation and a report, and the act was silent as to whether that report should be published or not. But if he reported that there was a prima facie evidence of a combine, a special commissioner was appointed; and the special commissioner's report was subject to exactly these provisions. From 1937 on, those provisions have been in the act.
That is, provisions for mandatory publication. Then he continues:
I submit that it is necessary that there be publicity. At least, it is my contention or submission that there should be publicity. This offence is not at all like an offence that speaks for itself. It is all a mystery. The public has no way of knowing whether there is any combine or not. It is not like theft, bank robbery, or any of those other overt or open acts where it is clear that there has been an offence. Here there is just a dark surmise and that is all. If the public is to know anything at all about this, it must be explained to them by the report of somebody who has made an investigation. If you have no provision that that report is to be made public, there is no possibility of an opportunity for public opinion to operate on governments, attorneys general or ministers of justice. There is no possibility of that; and you have to make a strong assumption that public officials will be fully alive to their responsibilities.
At that time Mr. Ilsley made it clear that he regarded the necessity of publication of the report as of first importance in connection with revealing trading activities that contravene the Combines Investigation Act. That, I suggest, is the answer to both the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), and to the Prime Minister, all of whom indicated that the reason there had been no publicity was that if publicity had been given there would have been a challenge to the government to prosecute, and that it would apparently put them into a difficult position.

On the same occasion, as reported at page 4920 of Hansard, I asked Mr. Ilsley this question:
I am not going to pursue the subject further, except to say that apparently the Attorney General of Canada, on receiving a report from one of the officials, under the Minister of Justice, in which definite findings are made of a combine, still has to be satisfied that the report which so indicates has a foundation for the conclusion reached by the commissioner.
Mr. Ilsley replied:
Absolutely; certainly he does. The Attorney General of Canada is not bound to do what the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act tells him. He is not obliged to take his facts, and he is not obliged to take his law. Presumably he will take his facts.
Those two excerpts from the words of the then minister of justice answer government spokesmen who say that the reason they did not give publicity to the report, and failed to carry out the mandatory provision, was one of two reasons-either that it would have given publicity that should not be given or, secondly, that the government would have been placed in a position where it would have to prosecute.
I do not think I am guilty of overstatement when I say that I know of no action by any government giving its support to private enterprise that will do more to undermine public belief in free and private enterprise than the fact that the publication of this report had been stifled until action can no longer be taken. If after producing the report according to law the explanation had been then made which has now been made, public opinion would have reacted either as against or in favour of the course pursued by the government.
I realize that, when discussing the question of combines, all too often it becomes a witchhunt wherein any wrongdoing on the part of private enterprise becomes the subject of bitter attacks. I believe in private enterprise. I want to see it preserved. Over the years, and particularly during recent years, it has been and still is being diminished almost everywhere in the world.
During two wars there has been regimentation in the economic world that has left the feeling that there is need for regimentation in the days of peace, and that by the simple exercise of state control all our economic problems can be solved. The result of control by the executive during two wars has been that people believe that the state can and does create wealth.
In discussing the need to amend the Combines Investigation Act, I believe that there is a happy medium between the British and American attitudes. The British attitude, so far as monopoly is concerned, is that unless such monopoly interferes with the rights of 45781-1111	>
Combines Investigation Act other producers, competitors or consumers, the bigness of a business should not of itself alone be ground for prosecution. [DOT] The attitude of the United States during recent years has been that the bigness of business in itself is an offence. In the last two years in the United States many prosecutions have been launched by the attorney general against great corporations whose paramount offence has been the size of the industries that have been proceeded against. All business is big as compared with what it was 20, 30 or 40 years ago.
The purpose in mind under combines legislation should be to provide equality of opportunity under the law so that every individual or number of individuals in our country may have the opportunity of risking capital in which the state is neither the insurer nor a partner. In other words, what a combines act should do is to provide equality under the law so that big and small businesses have equal access to markets and whereby the individual is protected against exploitation. Not only should the consumer be protected; the business competitor also should be protected. The purpose of anticombines legislation should be to assure that degree of fair dealing as between business and citizens of the state as will guarantee the greatest benefit for the greatest number.
One of the great criticisms of our system is that it lives by returning profit. Business requires profit. Profit is of prime importance to the maintenance of our way of life. The profit system spells our prosperity. Having said that, I believe that when any business or group of businesses operate in concert so as to injuriously affect either the consumer or other producers or prejudice the state, then the state has a responsibility to step under law to punish and prevent.
When amendments to the combines act were introduced three years ago the then minister of justice, now the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), indicated the need for something being done in order to improve the act, and amendments were introduced and passed. There have been several attempts to improve the combines act, one in 1937, one in 1923 and on one or two other occasions. However, no matter what amendments are made to the combines act, if the government of the day charged with the responsibility of carrying out the law regards political expediency as a justification to not follow the rule of law, then the law is meaningless.
In 1946 I believed that as a result of the changes made there would be protection of the Canadian people against what Mr. McGregor referred to in his recommendations regarding cartels as an illegal monopolistic trend that had grown up during the

Combines Investigation Act war, xhe result of which was to deny Canadian citizens that freedom from unjust trade practices that they should enjoy if private enterprise is to perform its function. In 1920 the former prime minister of this country used to refer to the "hidden hand of plutocracy".
He came to power in 1921. The exploitation by certain monopolies during the time the present government has been in power since 1921-there were five years during which they were out of power-has been such that every indication is given that the law has not been enforced. And I mean no reflection on Mr. McGregor. The law can be enforced only if those charged with the administration of justice carry out the recommendations of the commissioner.
The Minister of Justice is not bound by what the commissioner finds. He must examine what he says but he must publish the commissioner's findings. I do not want to appear to place it all on the shoulders of the Minister of Justice. Far be it from me to do that. The minister was merely the instrument whereby the government of this country acted in a manner that has not been duplicated since the days of King George III in 1763. Never since has any minister or any government dared to depart from the rule of law. Some there are who wrongly contend that there is one law for the powerful and another law for the weak, and the fires of such criticism are kindled when a thing like that is permitted to occur and when parliament views it with almost dispassionate disinterest.
Now we have another bill. The hidden hand of plutocracy which was spoken against in 1919 and 1920 must have been so hidden that it has not been discovered by the present government or its predecessors in office. I return to the tobacco prosecution, and I refer to that case, as I did to another, as a debacle. These companies had been convicted and an appeal allowed on a technical objection. I asked in 1946 why the government did not go ahead and prosecute again as the prosecutions had failed on technical grounds. The answer was that the war had come and at all events the companies had reduced their prices by ten per cent.
That was no excuse for not prosecuting. A law on the statute books unenforced is simply an invitation to wrongdoing. When there is a law on the statute books that requires a mandatory act to be done by the minister of any government and when the ministers of that government associate themselves with him in transgressing that law, then they encourage wrongdoing by prospective wrongdoers.


The support of this party has been indicated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) on the principles of the bill. I am not so sure that the doing away with the jury is a good principle. It is all very well to talk about the difficulty of making a jury understand; the fact is that juries can and do understand when there is wrongdoing that affects them under combines legislation. In Great Britain the company being tried has a right to trial by jury and in the United States it is mandatory. Why trial by jury is being taken away has not yet been explained by the minister to the satisfaction of all hon. members and it should be dealt with at greater length when in committee.
An amendment has been moved which I should like to summarize. It calls for the subject matter of the bill to be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records, and that it have power to report upon the extent to which effective administration of legislation relating to restrictive trade practices has been, or is being, prejudiced by the action of the government in failing to carry out the mandatory requirements of the existing law.
The leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) said that he would have liked a motion of censure. A motion of censure would have been a specific motion against one or more members of the cabinet, or the whole cabinet. What we are trying to get in connection with this legislation is the power to assure that the mistakes that have been made in enforcement in recent years, and the failure of the government to carry out the law, shall not be permitted to become the practice in this country. Let us submit the bill to a committee. What can we do there? We can get answers to certain questions that we cannot get in the house. We can bring Mr. Gordon before that committee and find out from him what minister gave him authority to place any industry above the law.
The leader of the C.C.F. group has asked for the production of some documents. One would think those documents would be right at hand. The cabinet has been able to consider the McGregor report since January. By this time they should have gathered the documents together, if there were any documents. Then we could have Mr. McGregor appear before the committee. The government says that it wants to put teeth in the law. Mr. McGregor wants teeth in the law. He is the one we should bring before this committee because, according to an outstanding member of the press, Mr. Austin Cross, in an article this morning, we cannot get

Mr. McGregor's side of the question until the end of the year because he is a civil servant, and therefore regards it as part of his bounden duty, and properly so, not to speak out. The newspaper report to which I have referred states:
1.	McGregor cannot talk directly to the press, but only to his minister.
Let us give him a chance to talk to members of parliament in a committee of parliament so that we shall get to the bottom of the controversy. The article continues:
2.	The minister cannot put forward McGregor's views since they are in conflict with the government's views which the minister must express.
Surely we want to relieve the minister of a difficulty such as that. One way to do that is to set up this committee, and the house will thereby relieve the minister of any responsibility for having to say things that cabinet solidarity denies him the right to say.

Combines Investigation Act which could be inquired into. These are things that the people of Canada have a right to know. These are things that parliament has the right to know. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest today to the previous speakers who have taken part in this debate on the bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act. It appears to me that we have listened to a good deal of crack oratory and the matching of nimble wits.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Crack or cracked?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I wanted to be polite and I said "crack". I trust that my speaking at this time will not be a case of a fool rushing in where angels fear to tread; for I do not claim to be a crack orator, neither have I much knowledge such as becomes the legal profession. But I have been doing a little reading lately in respect to monopolies and

combines and business in general, as well as reading the explanations that have been given by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the correspondence that went on between Mr. McGregor and the Minister of Justice.
I believe the bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act is worthy of support. I favour it. But I cannot quite convince myself that it goes far enough. It seems to me that the amendments are pretty well confined to the strengthening of the hands of the government for the purpose of prosecutions. That is all well and good as far as it goes. Whether or not it will take care of what sometimes happens in monopolies and combines in respect to unfair business practices I do not know, and perhaps it remains to be seen.
I once heard a speaker say something to this effect, that there was nothing wrong with a monopoly as such if it put on the market its production at cheaper consumer prices. I do not know that I altogether agree with that, but I have thought of the statement a good many times. All people are consumers and all would benefit even though it were a monopoly which put on the market production at a lower price to consumers. Perhaps there might be some confusion in respect of monopolies and combines.
I am not satisfied in my own mind that a monopoly and a combine are exactly the same thing. To all intents and purposes for argumentation I suppose we could put them together, but I think we should distinguish between them. I trust that I may not be accused of splitting hairs, but there may be a difference between a monopoly and a combine in this respect, that a monopoly, which term stems from another word, the Greek word "monos" which means first, all in one, or alone or single, put it whichever way you like, applies to a company which is the only one in that particular business.
That could constitute a monopoly. But a combine is just a little broader than that. A combine could consist of several business concerns in the same industry conniving and combining their efforts for a particular purpose. It seems to me that is the thing we are dealing with in the Combines Investigation Act.
We in this corner of the house believe in free competition. I believe that generally speaking the Canadian people believe in free competition, provided that free competition is also fair. We have been told over and over again that competition is the life of trade. I believe that we must maintain in Canada that same free competition, provided it is fair. For if we lose out here, then I
Combines Investigation Act am afraid we are losing the one great principle of freedom that has made democracies, and particularly the western free enterprise countries, the powerful nations that they are today.
However, perhaps it is not just as easy as that. Some interesting information came out from Washington the other day, where a house judiciary committee of congress is sitting investigating monopolies in the United States. A few days ago Mr. T. K. Quinn appeared before that subcommittee. Mr. Quinn was a former vice-president of the General Electric Company. A man of that status knows something about business. I should like to quote from a press dispatch one or two of the statements Mr. Quinn made to that committee. The press dispatch from Washington, November 3, states:
An excess of concentrated private economic power has fostered big government and big unions, and is driving this country towards socialism, T. K. Quinn, president of the T. K. Quinn Company, New York, told a house judiciary committee today.
I want hon. members to take note of what he said there, because it seems to me that if big business is not regulated in a fashion so as to see that it is fair in its competition, perhaps we shall be driven into state socialism. Another expression from this article is:
Mr. Quinn told the subcommittee, which is investigating monopolies, that the system of concentrated power in relatively few hands was "inconsistent and opposed to democratic objectives."
Then later on it states:
The ultimate safe solution to the problem of "bigness in business is physical and financial decentralization," Mr. Quinn advised the subcommittee.
Before Mr. Quinn had finished giving his evidence he made several proposals which he thought might help to deal with that situation. I place these proposals on Hansard only by way of passing them along to the appropriate authorities for consideration. I do not do so because I necessarily agree with all of them; in fact with one or two of them I do not agree. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) may take them for what they are worth. Mr. Quinn's proposals included the following:
1.	Banks and insurance companies would not be permitted resources in excess of-
-and the sum of a billion dollars is mentioned here. But of course that would be applicable to the United States.
2.	Officers and directors would not be permitted to serve for more than one private corporation for gain.
That is one proposal with which I agree, because it would put an end to that vicious thing known as interlocutory directorates.

Some adjustments might have to be made in that last one. Mr. Quinn however is only making suggestions which will help to stay the growing tendency toward centralization of business power in the hands of monopolies and combines.
There is another side to the picture, just the same, and I should like to offer some suggestions on that side. I now refer to an article headed "What Chance Has Small Business", appearing in the Reader's Digest. The writer is Samuel T. Williamson, formerly an editor of Newsweek and a staff writer of the New York Times. Mr. Williamson goes on to say that small business, to a very large extent, is the life of business in a nation. He does indicate that many small businesses at first go under, but he does not necessarily blame big business for putting them under, and states:
Sometimes a half million firms, most of them small, disappear in a year-sold, merged or just abandoned. Only one of two retail stores survives its first three years under the same management. Less than one store in three lasts more than seven years.
Then he goes on to say:
On the other hand, studies of retailing in-
Certain industrial states-
-show that the same mortality rates existed twenty and thirty years back.
Then he goes on to say that three economists who had analysed certain industrial districts discovered that stores did not last any longer a hundred years ago than they do now. Those facts are rather interesting. He goes on to say this:
In 1900 there were 21 firms for every 1,000 people. Today there are 26. And despite trends toward bigness, the average business firm has the same number of employees as at the beginning of the century.
Then he goes on to point out another rather interesting thing, that big business is sometimes dependent upon smaller business. He refers to one automobile company that buys


from nearly 1,100 different firms. One speedometer maker, one of those 1,100 firms, buys from 200 independent suppliers. That is an interesting thing to learn. Then he goes on to say:
Even when large concerns do a big proportion of the business in their line they encounter smaller firms' competition.
I know that that is not always true, but that is what he says. He continues:
When U.S. Steel was formed it controlled 65 per cent of steel production. Just before world war II its share was 38 per cent. Today it is 33 per cent.
I should like to read into Hansard two more paragraphs which I believe are important. He says:
Almost every big business one can think of started small. Small business is the hope and beneficiary of competitive enterprise. As long as there are people who would rather work for themselves even if it means working harder, and as long as small units can do some things better and cheaper than big ones, small business has a future. As long as competition is free and fair it need not fear big business.
Business freedom may be measured by these questions:	Are people free to invent new devices, to
bring out new products, to organize new services? Can people buy what they need from more than one producer or seller? And are the producers and sellers operating on a competitive basis? If so, small business-any business-is free.
I would point out to the Minister of Justice, who has the responsibility of administering this act, that I believe what Mr. Williams says there is true. It is the responsibility of the government through its Combines Investigation Act to see that competition is fair. I once heard President Roosevelt say something which has stuck with me throughout the years; he said that big business is not always bad business. I believe that, but I believe also that if big business becomes bad business, it is bad indeed. We cannot permit big business to become so powerful that it is above the government or above the law.
I do not want to be uncharitable, but it does seem to me that in the discussion that has taken place, in the report that has been submitted, in the correspondence and memoranda that have been exchanged, it is indicated that the milling industry of Canada had become so powerful that it could influence Mr. Gordon to offer it protection if it behaved itself. Perhaps that is putting it rather crudely. I am not making any criticism of Mr. Gordon because I believe he was the man for the job.
We know that he came in for considerable criticism during the war because many people regarded him as a dictator. I am not saying that he was because I never ran into conflict with him, but I do know that that was the opinion of some people. We do know that he was armed with all the power that a man needed in order to prevent inflation and bring prices into a reasonable position in respect to

trade and business. In that respect he was all-powerful, and yet it appears to me that we have a glaring example that he was not powerful enough to deal with a great industry without saying:	If you will help me here,
then you will be privileged.
I mention that in passing because unquestionably the evidence would indicate that that one big business was indeed a powerful business. I submit that the teeth of the Combines Investigation Act should be so sharp that big business that attempts to manipulate prices and distribute its product in such a way as to squeeze out small business can be dealt with. That is when big business becomes bad business, when it is able to so manipulate prices and so distribute its products as to squeeze out its weaker competitors. That sort of thing is inconsistent with our democratic way of life, a way of life which should grant to every man an equal opportunity to make good in business without fear of being destroyed by unfair business practices on the part of giant competitors.
We do know that there is a strong feeling among people that the big shot can get away with anything while the little man can get away with nothing. I do not think any business should be getting away with anything. Fair business is fair business. There is a feeling among people-I do not know whether it exists generally-that if a poor man steals a loaf of bread he is put in jail, but if the big shot steals a million dollars he is looked upon as being a rather brilliant and smart man.
I do not know that that would hold true in the administration of justice in Canada, but just the same that is what people think. A few years ago I met a man who had the experience of running for a seat in this House of Commons. He was waging his election campaign in the old days when he was on relief. He was a poor man, and during his campaign he wanted to get from one place to another, and he had to hitch-hike. Just as he was crossing a railroad track he saw a handcar sitting there and he said to himself, "I have no money, and there is a handcar. What does that add up to?" He got on the handcar and pumped his way for several miles to his destination, the next town.
The fact of the matter was that he was arrested and sent to jail. When he was running his election campaign a man in one of his audiences jumped up and said, "Are you bidding for our votes to enter the House of Commons?" He said, "Yes." The man in the audience said, "Is it not true you have been to jail?" That stumped him for a moment. Was he a jailbird? The way he answered was to say: "Yes, I have been to jail and I want to tell you the reason why I went to
Combines Investigation Act jail. I went to jail because I stole a handcar. That was my fatal mistake. Do you know what I should have done? What I should have done was to steal the whole railroad. I stole a handcar and was put in jail, but if I had stolen the whole railroad I would not be here asking you to vote for me because I might have been put in the Senate." In telling that story I cast no reflection on that august body, but that actually happened. You will want to know whether the man was elected. Believe it or not he was, and he sat in the house for a number of years.
What I am getting at is that the Combines Investigation Act must deal with business in such a way that it will guard the fairness of competition at all times. If there are any amendments needed to the Combines Investigation Act, I believe they must be made in order to strengthen the hands of the government in the administration of the act and in prosecutions under it. Believe me, unless there are prescribed penalties that will teach the powerful business tycoons that they must be fair, there is no use fooling around with the Combines Investigation Act at all. When I say they have to be taught and punishment must be meted out, I mean exactly that. There is little use in imposing on big business a fine of several thousand dollars or even $100,000. To my mind that is not punishment. I know that the minister may say that it is pretty hard to prescribe the particular punishment for an infraction of this law, but I believe it can be done.
I am not prepared now to say how it could be done, but I believe it could be done in such a way as to expose these men so that they will not get away with the attitude that, because they are business and financial tycoons, big shots, therefore they can do what they like. Their misdemeanours should be advertised high, wide and handsome. I do not know why their businesses should not immediately be put temporarily under the control of an administrator. Let the government step in with an administrator and advertise the actions of these men. They could advertise what they had done in newspapers and on the labels of the products if they wanted to do so. Let them advertise that the business is temporarily operated under a government administrator by reason of the fact that Mr. So-and-So, Mr. So-and-So, Mr. So-and-So, director So-and-So, President So-and-So have been guilty of unfair business practices. If there were teeth of that nature in the law then I think they would be pretty careful what they did.
I think I have said enough about the matter. I am in favour of the amendments to the bill, and I am saying that generally I think business in Canada is fair. I believe

Combines Investigation Act we can say that. I believe that the businessmen ot Canada have a desire to be fair and to do business legitimately, but if it is discovered that they are unfair in their business practices then let us call them to account for their actions and teach them in no uncertain way.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of supporting the amendment proposed by my leader, and I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that the proposal made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) is a reasonable one. The debate has disclosed that the matter is of a very grave, serious and fundamental nature. It affects the lives of everyone in the country and some outside of it.
A few days ago, speaking in another debate, I expressed the opinion that Canada was fortunate in that it had enjoyed good government. The events of the past few days compel me to modify that opinion, not only because of the revelation that a report, which by statute had to be made public within a fortnight, was kept secret from the public who are entitled to see it and also from the present session of the house and the session of the house held last spring, but also because of the contents of this report, and the contents of other reports that have preceded it, especially the one on the breadbaking industry in western Canada. I took the trouble to read a report of a committee of this house that was appointed in 1948 to investigate the rise in the cost of living. It is called the House of Commons committee report on prices.
In that report they drew attention to many practices they strongly condemned, and urged that the combines investigation commissioner should have greater funds at his disposal so that his department might be able to do greater work. Subsequently, on the recommendation of that committee, a royal commission was appointed which also approved of the work being done by the combines investigation commissioner and condemned certain practices which it learned were going on in this country and which were responsible for the rise in the cost of living.
Everyone in this country, rich or poor, no matter what his occupation, professional or layman, whether lawyer, doctor, fisherman, labourer, clerk or mechanic, is affected if there is a one point increase in the cost of flour. By every cent that flour rises everybody in Canada is affected. In my country we had no combines investigation act, and I was not familiar with the workings of this legislation. I do know, unfortunately, that some of the practices condemned in these reports, and which are illegal under the Combines Investigation Act, were carried

on in Newfoundland. I know, too, that during the war these flour companies which were selling at the ceiling price here in Canada under subsidies from the federal government were not selling at any ceiling prices in Newfoundland. Hon. members will be surprised to learn that we were paying from $17 to $20 a barrel for flour. There was no limit to the profits these flour companies could make in export trade. I know the combines investigation commissioner has attended international conferences whose aim was to prevent corporations such as these taking advantage of the public not only in their own country but in other countries as well, and I wish his attention had been directed to the prices being asked for flour in Newfoundland.

speechtext: He would have had no jurisdiction in Newfoundland; we did not have confederation then.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) says he would have had no jurisdiction in Newfoundland. Well, he would have jurisdiction now, and it would not be too late for him to come and make that investigation. Whether or not any investigation is made, we know now what they were being paid for wheat and flour in this country, and we know the profit that was being made in Newfoundland.
There are several things to which I take exception in these revelations, and which I think every hon. member, no matter what his party affiliations, must find reprehensible. The first is the suppression of the report. No justification has been presented to this house for withholding the report. It was a statutory obligation upon the Minister of Justice and the best that can be said in that connection is that he was prevailed upon by other, more influential members of the cabinet to withhold it. But then what about the interview described by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who had a question on the order paper asking if a report had been filed. The Minister of Justice went to his room in September and asked if he would mind withdrawing his question because the minister had some legislation to bring down and he would like to have the legislation ready at the same time the report was presented.
Who will deny that this is important legislation? Considering the seriousness with which hon. members regard this question, will anyone in this house deny that it is an important matter? Look at the publicity it has received across the country. Was there any mention of the amendment of the Combines Investigation Act in the speech from

the throne this session? Was there any mention of it in the speech from the throne last session? There was not; and why? It is evident that the government did not intend to do anything about the Combines Investigation Act until they were forced into it by the combines investigation commissioner, Mr. McGregor. The Minister of Justice tabled the memorandum and letter of Mr. McGregor and was willing to have them appear in Hansard. However, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) rose in his place and said, "No, I am not going to have it," and as acting leader of the government his will prevailed again. But when the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke here on Monday last he took advantage of the opportunity to read a contrary opinion into the records of this house. If the government were sincere and honest and earnest about these things, why should they resort to such subterfuges as I have just described?
During the discussion there was some crossfire, and some heated words were exchanged across the floor. How many hon. members remember the remark by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell)? He said, "What is all the fuss about? I had twelve officials of my department resign in one day. Why all this fuss about one official?" There is present this evening one hon. member who may remember back to 1910; I am referring to the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll). In January of that year another minister of labour rose in his place to introduce the very act we are discussing this evening. That minister of labour was none other than Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, who introduced the first Combines Investigation Act. Some hon. members, perhaps even some Liberal members, may not be familiar with the early history of Mackenzie King. He was especially chosen by the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier to attend every university at which he could acquire erudition-some knowledge on the subject of labour. Sir Wilfrid Laurier looked to the future, and he chose this man and sent him to Toronto, to Chicago, to Harvard, to Cambridge, so that he might acquire every possible bit of knowledge. Then Mackenzie King rose in his place in this house in 1910 and introduced the first Combines Investigation Act. At that time he said, "In this country and in the United States the people are noticing two phenomena, first a rise in the cost of living, and second an increase in the number of mergers and combines; and the people associate the two things. As the combines increase in number and in strength the cost of living goes up". Then he went on to give an elaborate
Combines Investigation Act account of the increase in the cost of living, together with an account of similar legislation in the United States and Europe.
That was the first Combines Investigation Act. It was to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies and trusts which might enhance prices or restrict competition to the detriment of purchasers. At that time Mr. Mackenzie King said the people had a right to look to the government for protection of their liberties. And despite what is sometimes said by my friends of the C.C.F., as in the days of old the people looked to the king to protect them against the strong, rich men, the "combine" men of those days, so today the people have a right to look to the government to protect their liberties. If the government should choose to protect the privileges of the rich men, then they do an injustice to the great majority of the people of this country.
The matter of the cost of living needs no elaboration today. There is no need to give any analysis of it, as Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King did in 1910. There is no need to doubt about combines and mergers today because we know they exist in greater number than ever. Mr. Mackenzie King said that, "unfortunately, human nature being what it is, we cannot believe that management considers primarily the good of a nation as a whole as opposed to those whose capital rests in their hands". Is that not an effectual answer to the statement of the Prime Minister when he referred to the patriotism of these great industrial magnates? In the course of my remarks, I shall have something to say which will cause hon. members to question whether or not those gentlemen were so patriotic as they have been represented to be.
Mr. Mackenzie King also suggested it was "the business of the government to see that no private interests are allowed to operate against the public good". Thirty-nine years have gone by since then, and many changes have occurred. There have been two world wars, kingdoms have fallen, and Mackenzie King is no longer active in the political life of this country. There is also the question of small businesses to consider. In 1924, there were 437 small mills operating in this country, and by small mills the combines commissioner means a mill producing less than
1,000	barrels of flour per day. In 1931, there were 372. In 1934, there was an increase to 435; but in 1947, the figures stood at 181. I say that is a serious indication that small businesses are gradually being absorbed by these great combines.
Now, what of Mr. McGregor? Who was he? Some bitter reflections were cast upon that gentleman by the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). I do not know what personal

Combines Investigation Act rancour exists between these two men. Perhaps hon. members are not aware of the fact that Mr. McGregor was a citizen of Ottawa, the son of a grocer in this city. He left school at the age of thirteen, and went to work in a newspaper office. After returning to school for some time, he worked in the post office and then for several years acted as private secretary to Mackenzie King. For six years, he acted in that capacity when Mr. Mackenzie King had become prime minister. When Mr. Mackenzie King needed a man to act as combines investigation commissioner, therefore, whom should he choose but Mr. McGregor, the man who had been trained under his eyes? For twenty-four years, Mr. McGregor has carried on his duties, as I understand, fearlessly, honourably and honestly. He is capable, efficient, and incorruptible. Men like that are few in any government. Shame on the government that did not make some effort to retain in its employ a man of that calibre. They allowed him to be sacrificed to the interests of these flour magnates, who are not the friends of this party but the friends of the government in power.
Is there a need for such legislation? The report of the commissioner is the answer. He says there is a greater need than ever. The report of the committee of this house on prices and the report of the royal commission all indicate the need for strengthening the power of the commissioner against these combines. In the last twenty-five years, there has been an enormous growth of these corporations. I know of one institution that has two business houses in this city, and since 1921 it has multiplied until it now has 121 in Ontario. Last year, it turned over $73 million. What small businessman could open a shop within half a mile of such a giant corporation? These are financial and commercial octopi that swallow every competitor coming within their reach. These chain stores and multiple stores are injurious to the economic health of this nation, and so are the combines.
To whom was it good news when the government suppressed this report, if not to the corporations named in this report? Do you not think the directors of these companies, the men whose names have been mentioned, shouted "Hurrah for the Liberal government that has stood by us; they are our friends"? Can anyone be blamed for believing that these men acted in that manner? Why did the government suppress this report? Does the Minister of Justice tell the prosecuting officers that they must not take action against other people accused of offences? Eleven companies operating flour mills across Canada had intentionally assisted in the formation and operation of a combine,

and yet they are not to be prosecuted. They cannot be prosecuted, in fact, because the report was suppressed until the two years prior of limitation had expired. Under the Criminal Code no prosecution can be launched two years after the alleged offence. I agree with the hon. member on my left who remarked that that provision of the Criminal Code should be amended to give greater latitude in the prosecution of combines.
Here is legislation which we are told has been recommended by Mr. McGregor, the man in whom the government no longer has confidence. The government must have been aware of the need of this legislation for some time. They must have been aware of the growing number of great corporations and the growing power of those corporations. No matter what amendments are passed at this session, those corporations will not fear such legislation when they realize that the government has practically ruled out the commissioner and suppressed his report condemning them.
An examination of this act raises two questions in my mind. Does it go far enough or does it go too far? Does it go too far against corporations who are so patriotic as to co-operate with the government in time of war? The member for Temiscouata, in his amusing speech, read out the names of the directors of some of the companies that were condemned. I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the report on the bread-baking industry in western Canada by Mr. Goldenberg, a special commissioner under the combines act. If hon. members have not read it, I recommend that they read it. If they will turn to page 100 of that report, they will find that two directors of the Ogilvie Company were conspiring on October 22, 1947, to put a man in northern Saskatchewan out of business. They bought him out for $100,000 and, if they had not done it, the Maple Leaf Company would have. Both these companies were in cahoots; they were combining to get that man out of business because he was an independent baker who was selling his goods at a price lower than the bakeries which these two giant corporations controlled.
If any honest man from Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, or British Columbia will read that report, he cannot help but condemn those two corporations. At least, he will then be able to understand why Mr. McGregor had reason for bringing in a report against this flour milling industry. For these are the same men who Mr. McGregor says have committed offences, and whom the government have chosen to exonerate.
The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) asked whether we could name a man. Well, there are two men. Their names

are right in the book on page 100. They are Mr. E. B. Frost and H. N. Davis, vicepresidents of Ogilvie Flour Mills. I do not care, Mr. Speaker, whether they are Tory or Liberal. Men who put up the price of flour or put up the price of bread and steal money from the poor, the poorest of this land, deserve no consideration whether they are Liberal or Tory or whatever they call themselves. They are not interested in the welfare of either party. They are interested only in themselves. They are selfish men. They want simply to have no competitors. They do not want to see anybody exist but themselves.
I think all hon. members, and especially the members of the government, must ask themselves this question: What is the state of this country? One would think sometimes that Canada is the only country in the world. One would think that there was no such place as Russia, where there are twenty million people who are slaves. One would think that there was no such place as China, where four hundred million people are being put under the control of the czar of Russia. It does not seem realistic sometimes to listen to the debates. All over the world there is a fear of the spread of communism. Have we no fear that communism will arise amongst us?
Czechoslovakia voted the communist government into power, and look at the condition of that country today. The other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) announced to the country, through this house, that he was permitting landlords to raise rents. Look at the furore that he raised at the same time all over this country. There were protests. Why were there so many protests? There were so many protests, Mr. Speaker, because, as he said himself, the majority of the people of this country were living in rented homes. I think he was wrong. I hope he was wrong because if that is the state of Canada then I fear for it, unless some influence is brought to bear to change the tide and help to get the people in their own homes. I know of small places in the district that I represent, and probably hon. members who represent rural ridings know the same thing, where every man owns his own home. Not a person is worried about whether the rents go up or down because there is nobody paying rent. They all own their own homes. They are independent men. They do not care what happens. But the men who live in the cities, the men who live in rented rooms, men and women who live in lodgings, are the people who are fearful. These people who are drawing their weekly or monthly salaries and who live on fixed incomes are the ones who are fearful. If the price goes up there may be penury or poverty for them.

I cannot see who is speaking but I know the remark is not a very intelligent one. What I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, is this. What we want to see is a stop to this growth of combines, and a stop to this growth of chain stores and multiple stores. We want to see small businesses increase all over the country so that there will be a greater number of small businesses and people will become more independent. Then the country would be a better country. There is a way to do it. It should be done through this committee or it may be done in some other way. But I would make a suggestion, as the hon. member who spoke before me suggested a number of methods. This is a suggestion for the Minister of Finance. There should be a tax according to the number of businesses that a man or a company has. If a company has one business it pays a small tax; with two businesses a little higher tax; with three a little higher, and so on. When they get into hundreds of businesses then they should pay a million dollars a year in taxes for having that privilege. That is the sort of thing I recommend. It may be a novel idea to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) but I ask him to think it over. Think it over, and see if there is not something in it. Some positive legislation must be enacted. The combines investigation commissioner admits that the act is not enough. The Minister of Justice knows that the act is not enough, and that is the reason he has brought in this legislation. But I will tell him now that he will not succeed even with this legislation. The cases take too long, and the owners of these businesses are watching. They are watching when the investigator comes around, and they report it to one another.
As the commissioner said himself, the flour mills did not put up their prices after September 15. They knew he was conducting an investigation and they were minding their

Combines Investigation Act p's and q's after that date. The individual is becoming more powerless every day. Before it is too late, before socialism or even communism should come to this country I ask the government to give serious consideration to some of the ideas that I have mentioned. Let us stop this strangling growth of giant corporations. If we do not we shall have socialism or we shall have the welfare state, the servile state it was once called, and it would mean the same thing. We may have security but we shall have no freedom. In this country we want to restore freedom of trade, freedom of competition, because there can be no liberty without economic liberty. That, Mr. Speaker, is a thesis for another speech and I do not think I should go on with it at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, big business has so few friends here tonight that my usual sympathy for the underdog almost convinces me that I should come to its defence, but since big business is not the question before us I shall have to leave my defence of it until some other time.
We are supposed to be debating the second reading of a bill that was moved this morning by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). While I have not found myself in general agreement with the minister in regard to the flour-milling report, I am bound to say that he made such a good job of explaining the amendments proposed in the bill that there is really nothing much left for me to do. The amendments proposed are three in number, and they are fairly simple. Indeed, so simple that I am puzzled why it took the Minister of Justice so long to introduce them into the house.
Having said that, I may as well go on with the discussion that has been in progress here since early this afternoon, namely, why the report made by the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act was not tabled in the house nor published. It did not have to be tabled in the house, but why was it not published within the requisite time provided by law.
I read the speech made by the minister last Monday, and really as a defence for not making the report public it is about the weakest thing that I ever read. I heard it as well as read it. But coming back to the proposed amendments he said-
If we get our amendment we will certainly be in a far better position as regards this or any other report than we are in now. I am going to base my request for support of the amendment on the position that I would not take the responsibility of prosecuting on any report unless we have this amendment.
I do not know what effect the amendments may have in regard to future reports, but if
{Mr. Browne (St. John's West).]

there is any validity in the opinion expressed last Monday night by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the amendments are certainly of no value so far as this report is concerned. Knowing what I do and, as I mentioned last Monday, that I was told that the draft of this bill was ready on September 21, I am inclined to the opinion that if Mr. McGregor had not resigned and forced the issue this bill would not be before us even now.

But that rather confirms my suspicion, that it was not until the minister had received the resignation that the notice was put in Votes and Proceedings. If it was the intention of the minister to introduce the bill in any case, then why was the introduction of the bill being held up? Surely it was ready quite a long time ago.
Speaking on Monday night the minister said:
One of a number of matters which I found upon my desk at that time was the report of the combines investigation commissioner in connection with the flour milling industry. I should like to lay before you, Mr. Speaker, and through you, before the members of the house, the situation as I then found it. I took this report which was upon my desk-a report which had not been delivered to me in person because I was not here to receive it, upon a matter about which I had no more personal information than I have about the present state of affairs in Siam-
Then he mentioned that he took the report to cabinet, and found that there was objection in cabinet to the report; and that objection arose, according to the information we have heard in the house, because Donald Gordon had made a statement, or the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had made a statement, that certain undertakings or instructions had been given to the milling companies during the war years.
But is it not strange that apparently between the time the minister came into his office after his election in January, 1949, up until October 22, there was no effort made to bring together those people, Mr. McGregor, Mr. Gordon, and others, who could explain what it was all about? If the minister did not know anything more about the report than he knew about the state of affairs in Siam, surely there was a man in his department who knew something about the report. Surely Mr. McGregor knew something about the report-and Mr. McGregor would have been

glad to explain the report to him. As a matter of fact I rather think Mr. McGregor knew more about the report than the Minister of Trade and Commerce did; and if Mr. McGregor had been consulted perhaps he could have told the minister that there was no reason in the world why the report should not be made public. If there was a reason, perhaps the minister could have induced the commissioner to give him a written statement to the effect that the report should not be published at that time.
We come to another point. If the minister did not know what to do with the report in January, 1949, he did know that the law required him to make the report public. He knew that parliament was meeting on January 26, and he could have come to parliament at that time saying that he had this report and that for certain reasons he did not want to make it public until he could amend the Combines Investigation Act.
Surely that would have been the logical and reasonable thing to do. Parliament had neither to prorogue nor to be dissolved on April 30. We could have stayed here until we had amended the Combines Investigation Act so that, as the minister has said-
-we will certainly be In a far better position as regards this or any other report than we are In now.
Had the minister done that, the milling companies could have been taken into court, because I understand that was prior to the expiration of the two years' time limit in which prosecutions could be started. There does not seem to me to be a single out for the minister-not a single out. It has been said that he has been hiding the report. I do not say he was hiding it, but he certainly did nothing to bring it to light.
Then we come to the replies he gave to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) at the conclusion of his speech. At page 1524 of Hansard we find this:

speechtext:
There have been several references tonight to free enterprise. I do not know whether those who made those references realized that the purpose of the Combines Investigation Act is to keep enterprise free. What is wrong today with free enterprise is that those who are advocating free enterprise do not believe in free enterprise. They believe in monopolies and combines. That is why I have a file of reports so thick that it is a burden to carry downstairs, all of them showing how certain industries combine for one purpose or another.
We had an investigation a little while ago into the bread-baking industry and I should like to read a little bit of the evidence from

that report to show how fond free enterprisers are of free enterprise. This evidence was taken in Winnipeg. The witness was Mr. Conrad, and in the report I find the following:
Q. The Commissioner:	Did Mr. Addems have
authority to cut off supplies from Safeways, if they did not maintain the price?
A. I don't think he would do it.
Q. Did any such incident arise in connection with any retailer who didn't maintain your price?
A. There was one instance, if I remember correctly. That was with Safeways. They wished to sell our bread at one cent less than the other stores sold it for. We couldn't agree to that, we were price minded, and we lost business because we couldn't agree to it.
They lost business because they would not sell to Safeways. It continues:
Q. They were prepared to pay you the wholesale price and they wanted to sell it at a lower price than your other customers?
A. Yes.
Q. That being contrary to policy, you refused to sell them unless they were prepared to do as the others did?
A. Yes, that is right.
I wonder if that is free enterprise. The next item of evidence to which I wish to refer was taken in Vancouver, and is found on page 302 of the evidence:
The policy was also confirmed in evidence by Mr. Colwell, of Canadian Bakeries, as follows:
Q. What does bread retail at in the stores in Vancouver?
A. Eleven cents.
Q. What would you do if one of the retail stores should sell at 10 cents?
A. We would refuse to serve him.
Q. That would be your policy?
A. Yes. As a matter of fact I might add that has been the policy of the company ever since I have been with them. 1 started with them in 1912. Shellys first and then Canadian Bakeries, since 1912. I don't know of any single day we have not maintained the retail sale of our bread.
Q. That has been the policy of the company all the way through?
A. Yes it has.
Q. You have never weakened?
A. We could have held Safeways if we had let them sell at ten when the price was advanced: we told them we wouldn't do that and we didn't serve them.
The above quotations are to be found on page 81 of the report on the bread-baking industry in western Canada. Turning to the next page, and again in British Columbia, under the heading of "Agreements on tenders", the report reads:
As in Alberta and Saskatchewan, the bakers in British Columbia discussed and agreed upon uniform tenders for the provision of bread to the armed services.
The Minister of National Defence, whoever he was at that time, would ask for tenders for bread. They would go to great pains to advertise, and the particular bakeries would get together and decide on the price at which
Combines Investigation Act they would sell bread to the army, or sell bread to the people of Canada. The report goes on:
On December 17, 1941, Mr. G. R. Law, manager of Weston's, Victoria, wrote to Mr. Conrad:
"We have sent in the army tender for the contract January 1 to March 31 at 5 cents. Our last contract was for 51 cents. You will remember we discussed this on your last visit. Mr. Land of Canadian Bakeries and myself discussed this very carefully before submitting the tender and decided that with so much cheap bread around and with Vancouver bakers dropping their price we would be better to go to the five cent price. Our tender had to be in before I could get anything definite on what the Vancouver bakers were going to do although I had been advised that they were going to 4-90 at least. The tender, by the way, has been accepted.''
That letter was exhibit 405 in the inquiry. Then we come to July 2, 1943, when Mr. Conrad of Weston's wrote to Mr. B. M. Colwell, manager of Canadian Bakeries, Vancouver. I think this quotation will show whether the prices board was making agreements to keep up prices. It reads:
The food administrator at Ottawa is complaining and has complained to officers of our parent organization that there is in Vancouver in effect a combine to regulate and keep up the price of bread to the army. Furthermore, he is sending Mr. Malkin to Vancouver to investigate the situation. I believe it would be a good idea if all the members of the association would get together and work out their ingredient, factory, administrative and shipping container costs, etc., so that they will be in a position to have time to discuss their own costs and be able to prove when the time comes-
That is, when Mr. Malkin arrives in Vancouver.
-that the price of 4-75 cents per pound is justified. To my mind there will be no difficulty about this whatsoever. One point which I believe to be very important is that since the bakeries have enjoyed a higher volume of business by their own right, the army volume of business is baked in overtime which would have effect of increasing labour costs. In my own mind and as far as our organization is concerned, there is nothing wrong with the price quoted to the army, considering the local conditions in effect at both Vancouver and Victoria.
Surely with all the information on the flour milling case that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) could have had by requesting it, and with experts to explain it to him, there was no necessity for him to take the advice of people who did not know anything abo.ut it. If he had only read the letter that accompanied the report from Mr. McGregor he would have found that the investigation was begun in September, 1947, that hearings were held in Winnipeg in October and November, 1947, and in Toronto and Montreal in January, February and March, 1948. The second last paragraph of the letter reads:
At my request counsel for the commission prepared a detailed summary of and commentary on the evidence which I then sent to the companies and persons involved as notice of the matters

Combines Investigation Act alleged. At the same time they were invited to supplement in any way they wished the representations and evidence already given during the hearings in regard to the same matters. Full opportunity was then given for those involved to present such further representations and evidence. Written or oral argument was then presented by or on behalf of all to whom notice had been given. In some instances the argument was directed primarily to a claim that the commissioner had acted without jurisdiction and without giving them adequate notice. On June 4, 1948, further hearings were held before me in Ottawa during which argument was heard from an officer of one company and its counsel.
In no case did these companies claim or bring forward proof that there were any understandings or instructions from the wartime prices and trade board or from any officer thereof. I suggest to the minister and to the government that they accept the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition and allow the matter to go to a committee where we can bring all those together who have different ideas on these matters, where we can get their evidence under oath, if necessary. Then we can come to our own conclusion as to who is right and who is wrong. Until that is done we shall not know who is right and who is wrong.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The only applause I get when I rise to speak is the word "question" from my good friends across the way. This debate has taken a course which greatly interests me. One of the most interesting things I have heard, I think, is the story of a friend of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) stealing a handcar. I know something about handcars; I earned my living pushing one all one summer when I was seventeen. The hon. member's friend must be a powerful man, because one man cannot push a handcar if there is the slightest bit of grade. So I think probably his friend preferred jail to pushing the handcar; in any event he would if he were smart.
There is something I am very anxious the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) should answer when he comes to close this debate. The thing that is bothering me is why we need the Combines Investigation Act at all.
I refer hon. members to sections 498 and 498A of the Criminal Code, and I think perhaps the minister will admit that I should have some knowledge of this because in a case which has been much discussed here, known as the tobacco case, I was prosecutor until I was fired by the premier of Alberta, who at that time was also attorney general.
I was not fired for knowing nothing about it; nevertheless I was fired. Then the gentleman who is now chief justice of Ontario, whose name I believe is McRuer, was paid by this government to prosecute the case;

Combines Investigation Act fifteen days after it was delivered. I do not know that I have ever felt more sorry for a man in my life than I do for him. The minister has been ill-advised, and at law what is he doing now? He is pleading guilty, and then calling the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to give evidence of character and extenuating circumstances. That is the simple position in which this house finds itself at the moment.
What is all this difficulty about? The ministers frankly disagree with one another, then drive one another home to dinner and that ends that. They laugh it off in this house. They are not the people who are really at cross-purposes. Their difficulty was a simple one; shall be publish it or shall we not? Shall we break the law or shall we not? Let us break the law because we will bring in some amendments and morally we shall be free. Legally, they are in breach of a mandatory statute. The two men who are really interested are McGregor and Gordon. McGregor says, I do so and so, and he puts it in writing to the minister. He leaves it on the minister's desk, which is all he is entitled to do.
Mr. McGregor was entitled to say that, in his judgment, this report should not be made public. Apparently, without any cloudiness in his eyes or in his brain, he decided not to so recommend. His failure to do that put the minister in a spot, Mr. Speaker; there is no doubt about that. The minister had only recently arrived from a little place called Winnipeg, which is neither east nor west, and never the twain shall meet until earth and sky stand presently, and all that sort of thing. The minister was faced with this difficult problem. He was the junior member of the cabinet. These big boss boys who have been here for some time said, "Stuart, do not do it; we might get into difficulty". The minister said "Where do I go from here?" Ten months later these bosses said, "Publish the thing because McGregor has resigned". No one knows how I get these secrets from the cabinet but, really, that is about what took place.
The difference is really between Mr. McGregor and Mr. Gordon. Let us get McGregor and Gordon before a committee, leaving out the sin of omission which at law, as the Minister of Justice knows, is often worse than a sin of commission. Who are the people who meet head on over this whole business? It is Donald Gordon and Fred McGregor, that is who they are. One said so-and-so and the other said something quite to the contrary. One says the whole thing is excusable because he told these companies, both verbally and in writing, that they were free of the Combines Investigation Act for as


long as the wartime prices and trade board was in existence-not for the period of the war, but as long as prices were under the control of that board.
A request has been made for that correspondence. It has not been produced. A memorandum from Donald Gordon has been produced. I am not criticizing anybody. I do not do that until I get the facts. I will admit that Donald Gordon is perhaps the best Scotch singer of whom I know in Ottawa. When it comes to his judgment of the Combines Investigation Act, however, I want to know what he knows about it. I should like to know whether he was accurate in the memorandum which he gave to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and which the Minister of Trade and Commerce, through the great kindness of his heart and nothing else, read to the little children of this house. We are to accept the crumbs that fall from our master's table and we are supposed to be well satisfied.
I have outlined what the amendment requests, that we might have a committee in which we humble members of parliament might be able to ask these great civil servants a few simple questions. Is that unreasonable? Is there anybody on the Liberal side who would suggest to me that that is unreasonable? Remember, I know that in the back of your minds you all have the idea that the man who is talking is seeking to do some terrible thing politically, or something of that sort. But there are limits in these committees. We have good chairmen of these committees. I would suggest that the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), who I think is one of the fairest chairmen of committees that I have ever known-and that is no reflection on anyone else, but he is tops- be made chairman of the committee. Then, let us get Fred McGregor; let us get Donald Gordon. They differ in this thing and in various things. And let us, the members of the House of Commons, find out what the true situation is. There can be no ministerial difficulty about it, because either of these men is right or he is wrong. The story we get from them is this. First, Gordon says that in a limited period he gave these undertakings verbally and in writing. Well, he can tell us to whom he gave them. If they are in writing he can produce the letters that he wrote. If they are oral he can tell us. In the meantime, little McGregor, little wee McGregor as he is now, not what he was just a few weeks ago, can give us the reasons in some detail for his resignation. That is all the amendment means. Is there anybody who will suggest that that is unreasonable in any way?

What is the other side? We won't grant a committee. We won't permit these questions to be asked. We won't have these men meet one another-I trust face to face. I believe they are very good friends even now, but one of them can be mistaken. Let us put it on the best ground we can. Let us find out which one is mistaken or which one perhaps is being even more than mistaken. And then let the members of the House of Commons form a judgment on the whole matter.
I turn now to another aspect of the amendment itself. I hope the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will correct me if I have misinterpreted the meaning of the section dealing with evidence. As I remember it, the old law of the scoop shovel method, which was backing a truck up and throwing everything up on the judge's desk, came from a case about twenty or twenty-five years ago from the same court of appeal in Ontario. It was Rex v. Clark or some such short name. I am not sure of it, but it was an appeal court case, and that is where we got into this habit of trying to prove things in that way.
May I say to the lay members of the House of Commons that you do not need to have conspirators all in one place or have them together. You may convict people of conspiracy who have never seen one another or have never heard of one another. That is part of it. You first show that there is a conspiracy and then here we go gathering nuts in May, and you pick them in Siam or in London or in any other place. They have never seen each other, and yet under our law they may be guilty of conspiracy.
I am going to say this to the Minister of Justice. We should exercise the greatest care in finding a man guilty before trial. Let me say at once I agree with him that the amendment to the statute says that what the government seeks is the rebuttal presumption. That of course means that I am guilty but I may have a chance to prove myself innocent. That is exactly what the rebuttal presumption is. I often think that perhaps the further we wander from the great rule of English law that a man is innocent until he is proven guilty the more we incur grave, perhaps not consequences but, I fear, consequences which may arise from something like that. Under the Criminal Code the only one that I remember at the moment is one that I am in hearty agreement with, namely, in connection with drugs. I am in hearty agreement with the principle that in the case of any person found in possession of drugs we should say to him, you are guilty unless you prove yourself innocent. But with great respect, Mr. Speaker, I cannot-perhaps it is my training
Combines Investigation Act in law-say other than that I find it difficult to accept the idea which is inherent in this bill that we need to depart from the old idea of innocence until guilt is proven. I repeat what I said a moment ago.

speechtext: In his prosecution of the tobacco combines in Edmonton did he not himself as prosecutor invoke this possessory principle in getting admitted as evidence these truckloads of documents which he brought to that trial?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Oh I did, yes, but I failed to have them admitted as evidence. They were all marked for identification; and when I explained to His Lordship and asked him, which was quite nervy for counsel, why they were not marked in evidence, he told me that I had a lot of experience at the bar and that I should know. I then went to the attorney general of Alberta and suggested that we have a stay, that I could not get any further with the rulings I was getting from the judge. I was relying on that Ontario case of which I spoke.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I am not implying any criticism of my hon. friend as counsel. I was just asking for information as to whether in that case he did not invoke the same possessory principle which he now decries in this bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
No. May I make myself very plain about this. At the moment I was not discussing that. I was discussing the rebuttal presumption. I had finished dealing with the evidence. The minister will remember I did say that I could call and did call officers of these various corporations who explained whose signature that was, what his job was, what an executive was, what his position was, what his authority was; in fact, the difficulty that the minister ran up against in the dental case. I still say that the officers of these corporations are available. If they are dead they have successors who are quite capable of telling whose signature this is and the other is, what his position was and the authority he had to carry on the corporation's business. When I was interrupted by the minister-and I welcomed it because I am trying to be helpful; I hope the minister will interrupt me if I make any mistakes-I was turning back to the old principle of the rebuttal presumption which is contained in the bill. As I say, under the Criminal Code
